Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 1:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra. These are the verses of the Book; and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe (1)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the interpretation of His words ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ and ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra﴾, and their counterparts among the letters of the alphabet with which some of the opening chapters of the Qur'an begin, earlier, sufficiently so that they need not be repeated [[See what has preceded: 1:205–224 / 6:149 / 12:293, 294 / 15:9, 225, 549.]]. However, we will mention the reports that are specific to each surah whose beginning contains some of them.

Among the reports on this matter concerning this surah, from Ibn Abbas, transmitted by Abu al-Duha Muslim ibn Subaih and Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him, is the distinction between the meaning of what begins its first verse, with the addition of the letter Mim that it contains over all the other surahs that begin with ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "over all the other surahs of those beginning with Ra", and the correct reading is what I have confirmed.]], and the meaning of what begins its sister surahs [[The context: "... the distinction between the meaning of what begins its first verse ... and the meaning of what begins its sister surahs".]], with that part missing from them.

The transmission of this from him:

2004४4- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Hushaym, from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra﴾ he said: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing."

2004५5- Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu al-Duha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra﴾ he said: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing."

2004६6- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra﴾: they are openings with which He begins His speech.

* *

As for His words: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, the meaning is: these, which I have related to you the account of, are the verses of the Book which I sent down before this Book which I have sent down to you, to those to whom I sent down My messengers before you.

* *

It has also been said: what is meant by that is the Torah and the Gospel.

Those who said this:

2004७7- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra. These are the verses of the Book﴾: the Books that were before the Qur'an.

2004८8- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, he said: the Torah and the Gospel.

* *

As for His words: ﴿and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [the Qur'an], then act upon what is in it and hold fast to it.

The people of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said this:

2004९9- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid: ﴿and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾, he said: the Qur'an.

20050. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿and that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾: i.e., this Qur'an.

* *

Regarding His words ﴿and that which has been sent down to you﴾ there are two grammatical possibilities:

The first: the nominative, on the basis that it is a new independent statement, so that it is in the nominative case as the subject of "the truth" (al-haqq) and "the truth is with it" (al-haqq bihi). On this reading is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah which we mentioned earlier from them.

* *

The second: the genitive, by conjunction to "the Book" (al-kitab), so that the meaning of the sentence then becomes: these are the verses of the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an. Then "the truth" (al-haqq) begins a new clause meaning: that is the truth, so its nominative case is by an implied element of the speech that is dispensed with because the apparent sense indicates it.

* *

If it were said: the meaning of that is: these are the verses of the Book which has been sent down to you from your Lord, the truth; the conjunction "and" was introduced before "that which" (alladhi), though it is a qualifier of "the Book", just as the poet introduced it in his saying:

To the king, the lordly one, and the son of the champion,
and the lion of the battalion in the crowd

and he conjoined with "and", all of it being the attribute of one person, this would be a valid line of interpretation.

However, if it is interpreted in this way, then the correct reading of "the truth" (al-haqq) is the genitive, as an attribute of "that which" (alladhi).

* *

As for His words: ﴿but most of the people do not believe﴾: but most of the people among the polytheists of your people do not affirm the truth that has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not acknowledge this Qur'an and what it contains of its clear verses.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 2:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the One who raised up the heavens without pillars that you can see; then He established Himself upon the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He arranges the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says: Allah, O Muhammad, is the One who raised up the seven heavens without pillars that you see, and made them a roof, raised up over the earth.

* *

"Al-'amad" is the plural of "'amud" (pillar), and it refers to the columns and whatever a building is supported by, as the poet al-Nabigha said:

"And subdue the jinn, for I have given them leave / to build Tadmur with smooth stones and pillars"

[[Diwan: 29; Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 320; Shams al-'Ulum of Nashwan al-Himyari: 37; and many others, from his famous poem in which he apologized to al-Nu'man when they slandered him regarding the matter of al-Mutajarrida. Before it he says: "I see no one among people who resembles him, nor do I exempt any one of the peoples / except Sulayman, when God said to him: / 'Rise up in the wilderness and mark its boundaries away from the desert.'"

His saying "wa khayyis al-jinn" means: subdue and tame them. "Al-Sifah" are thin, broad, hard stones.

"Tadmur" is a city in Syria. Nashwan al-Himyari said in Shams al-'Ulum: "The city of Syria is built of huge rocks, and in it is a wondrous construction. It was named Tadmur after the Amalekite queen, the daughter of Hassan ibn Udhayna, because she was the first to build it. Then Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon him, dwelt there after that, and the jinn built for him there a great edifice, and the Jews and Arabs attributed its construction to the jinn, because they considered it so magnificent."

This is a good text from their reports and stories in the pre-Islamic period.]] The plural of "'amud" is "'amad," just as "adim" is the plural of "adim" (hide); and if it were pluralized with a damma, saying "'umud," it would also be permissible, just as "rasul" is pluralized as "rusul" and "shakur" as "shukr."

* *

He said: What would make you know? Perhaps they are with pillars that you do not see.

* *

Whoever interprets it this way intends the Arabic practice of moving the negation from the end of the sentence to its beginning, as the poet said (Ibn Harma):

"I do not see it ceasing to be unjust / to bring me a calamity and to wound me with it"

[[Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni 277, 279, from nine verses; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' on the interpretation of the verse; al-Adddad of Ibn al-Anbari: 234.

It is claimed that Ibn Harma was told: "Quraysh do not pronounce the hamza," so he said: "I shall compose a qasida in which I pronounce the hamza throughout in the dialect of Quraysh," and its opening is: "Indeed Sulayma, by God, guards her / she withheld something that he did not withhold..."]]

He means: "I see her not ceasing to be unjust," so he placed the negation away from its position before "tazal," as another said: [[I do not know who said it.]]

"When the times please you with a state from a man / leave him, and entrust his state to the nights"

[[Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' on the verse; al-Adddad of Ibn al-Anbari: 234. His saying "wakil halah" means: leave his affair to the nights, from "wakala ilayhi al-amr," i.e., he referred the matter to him. His saying "they come upon what was good of him" means they overpower the good of his affair and take it away. "Al-ali" means the one who falls short.]]

"They come upon what was good in him / even if it was in what people do not see as falling short"

He means: even if among what people see, he does not fall short.

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views is to say as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is the One who raised up the heavens without pillars that you see﴾, so they are raised without pillars that we see, as our Lord, exalted is His praise, said. There is no report to the contrary, nor any proof obligatory to accept beyond it. [[That is, with precision, understanding, intellect and piety, which Abu Ja'far employed in his exegesis.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, it means: He rose over it.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "istiwa'" and the disagreement of those who differ concerning it, and the correct view among what they said about it, with its evidences, earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See the explanation of "istiwa'" earlier: 1:428–431; 12:482–483; 15:18. And the explanation of "al-'Arsh" earlier: 15:245, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

His saying: ﴿and subjected the sun and the moon﴾ means: He set the sun and the moon moving in the sky, subjecting them within it for the benefit of His creation, and made them submissive for their benefits, so that by their movement in it people may know the number of years and reckoning, and distinguish by them between night and day.

* *

His saying: ﴿each running for a specified term﴾: Exalted is His praise says: all of that runs in the sky, ﴿for a specified term﴾, that is, for a known time, and that extends to the end of this world and the establishing of the Resurrection, at which time the sun will be wound up, the moon will be eclipsed, and the stars will fall.

And that was omitted from the speech, because the listeners who belong to the tongue in which the Qur'an was revealed understand its meaning, and because "kull" (each) necessarily requires a complement to what it encompasses. [[See the explanation of "kull" and its rules earlier: 15:540, note 1, and the references there. And see what Abu 'Ubayda said in Majaz al-Qur'an 1:321.]]

* *

The people of interpretation said the same as what we said regarding His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾.

[[His saying "the world" seems to mean the perishing of the world; he restricted himself to mentioning "the world," because it is known by necessity of religion that it is perishing, and eternal life is only in the Hereafter.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 3:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth and placed therein firm mountains and rivers. And from all fruits He made therein two mates, two. He causes the night to cover the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.﴾ (13:3)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His mention, says: And Allah is the One who spread out the earth, stretching it lengthwise and widthwise.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and placed therein firm mountains﴾, He, glorified is His praise, says: He placed in the earth mountains that are steadfast.

* *

And "rawasi" is the plural of "rasiyah," which means steadfast. It is said from it: "arsaytu al-watad fi al-ard" (I drove the peg into the ground) when I fixed it firmly, as the poet said: [This is al-Ahwas.]

Bihi khalidatun ma yarimna wa hamidun ... wa ash'atha arsathu al-walidatu bil-fahri

[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:321, and al-Lisan (r-s-a). His version is "sawa khalidat" and "tarsihi al-walidah." "Al-khalidat" and "al-khawalid" are the stones of the cooking-hearth, so named for their long endurance after the traces of the abodes have decayed. "Ma yarimna" means they do not leave their places, from "ram al-makan yarimuhu," when one departs from it. "Al-hamid" is the ash compacted one upon another. "Al-ash'ath" is the peg, because its head is pounded so that it becomes frayed and split, and "al-walidah" is the young girl, and "al-fahr" is a stone the size of a palm, with which one pounds.]

He means: fixed it firmly.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and rivers﴾, it means: He placed in the earth rivers of water.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿And from all fruits He made therein two mates, two﴾, the "min" in His saying ﴿and from all fruits﴾ is connected to the second "ja'ala" (made), not the first.

* *

The meaning of the statement is: He made therein two mates, two, from all fruits. By ﴿two mates, two﴾ is meant: from every male, two, and from every female, two; that makes four, two males and two females, according to the view of some.

* *

We have already explained earlier that the Arabs call the pair "zawjayn" (two mates), and a single male "zawj" for its female, and likewise a single female is "zawj" and "zawjah" for its male, to the extent that there is no need to repeat it in this place. [See the explanation of "al-zawj" earlier, 1:397, 514 / 7:515 / 12:184 / 15:322-324.]

This is made clearer by the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ [Surah al-Najm: 45], so He called the two, the male and the female, "zawjayn" (pairs).

He only meant by His saying ﴿two mates, two﴾ two kinds and two types.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿He causes the night to cover the day﴾, it means: the night envelops the day, clothing it with its darkness, and the day the night with its light. [See the explanation of "al-ighsha'" earlier, 12:483 / 15:75.] As:

20066- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿He causes the night to cover the day﴾, i.e., He clothes the night over the day.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought﴾, He, exalted is His mention, says: Indeed in what I have described and mentioned of the wondrous creation of Allah and His great power by which He created these things, there are proofs, arguments, and admonitions for a people who reflect upon them, so that they draw inference and take heed from them, and thereby know that worship is not fit nor permissible except for the One who created and arranged them, not for other deities and idols that have no power to harm or benefit, nor for anything else, except for the One who originated that and brought it into being from nothing, blessed and exalted is He; and that the power by which He originated that is the power by which He is not incapable of reviving those of His creatures who have perished, restoring what has passed away from them, and originating whatever He wills to originate. [Context: "and that is the power by which He is not incapable..." ]

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and crops, and palm trees, both clustered and single, watered with one water; yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Surely in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ (13:4)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: His mention, exalted is He, ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾ means: in the earth there are portions of land near one another, close to each other in their adjacency. They differ in their excellence despite being neighbours and close to one another. Among them is a salty tract (sabakha) that grows nothing, next to a good tract that grows and yields.

The readers differed regarding the recitation of his words ﴿And crops and palm trees﴾. The majority of the readers of Medina and Kufa recited it: ﴿وَزَرْعٍ وَنَخِيلٍ﴾ with a genitive (khafd), joining it by coordination to "vines" (a'nab), meaning: in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and of crops, and of palm trees.

Some readers of Basra recited it: ﴿وَزَرْعٌ ونَخِيلٌ﴾ with a nominative (raf'), joining it by coordination to "gardens" (jannat), meaning: in the earth are neighbouring tracts and gardens of vines, and in them also are crops and palm trees.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this is to say that these are two readings close in meaning, and each of them has been read by well-known readers. So whichever of them a reader recites, he is correct.

This is because "crops and palm trees," when they are in gardens, are in the earth, and when they are in the earth, the earth in which they are is a garden. So it is the same whether they are described as being in a garden or in land.

* * *

As for his words ﴿and palm trees, clustered and single﴾:

Indeed, "ṣinwān" (ṣinwān) is the plural of "ṣinw" (ṣinw), which refers to palm trees that share one root, and their singular and dual forms are not distinguished in the nun except by inflection (i'rab). That is, the nun in its dual form is always kasra, while in its plural form it varies across the cases of inflection. A parallel to it is "qinwān" (qinwān), whose singular is "qinw" (qinw).

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):**

20111. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah informed me, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿ṣinwān﴾ (clustered palms): "Three palm trees on one root, like three brothers and sisters of one mother and father who differ in their works, just as the fruit of these three palm trees on one root differ." Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: "Like the righteous and wicked of the children of Adam, whose father is one."

20112. Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah informed me, from Mujahid, similarly. [[The report 20112: "Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Akhnasi." I have not found his grandfather's name mentioned except in this report. I have previously discussed the verification of his name in reports 10758 and 10759, and the references there.]]

20113. Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah, from al-Hasan, who said: "This is a parable that God struck for the hearts of the children of Adam."

The earth was, in the Hand of the Merciful, one clay. He spread it out and flattened it, and the earth became adjoining pieces. Water descends upon it from the sky, and so this [piece] brings forth its blossoms, its fruit, and its trees, and that [piece] brings forth its plants and revives its dead land, while this [piece] brings forth its salt flats, its brine, and its filth. Yet both are watered with one water.

If the water were salty, it would be said: "These have become barren only because of the water!" Likewise, people were created from Adam, and reminder descends upon them from the sky. So some hearts soften, becoming humble and submissive, while other hearts harden, becoming heedless, forgetful, and distant.

Al-Hasan said: "By God, no one sits with the Qur'an without rising from it with an increase or a decrease." God said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers in nothing except loss﴾ [Surah al-Isra' 17:82]. The scholars did not mention his narration from al-Hasan, yet he is worthy of being narrated from. It has passed as numbers 10334 and 10335. His statement "istasbakhat" (they became barren/salty) is something that should be added to the derivatives of "sabakhah" in the lexicon books.]]

* *

As for His statement ﴿watered with one water﴾ (tusqā bi-māʾin wāḥid), the reciters differed regarding His statement ﴿tusqā﴾.

The majority of the reciters of Medina, Iraq, Kufa, and Basra read ﴿tusqā﴾ with a ta' (tuqsā), meaning: the gardens, the crops, and the palm trees are watered. Some of them said: ﴿tusqā﴾ was said with a ta' only because of the feminine gender of "grapevines" (aʿnāb).

* *

Some of the Meccans and Kufans read ﴿yusqā﴾ with a ya' (yusqā).

* *

The grammarians differed regarding the reason for the masculine form when it is read this way, since it is a predicate about the gardens, grapevines, palm trees, and crops: that they are watered with one water.

Some grammarians of Basra said: when it is read with a ta', it refers to "grapevines," just as the livestock (anʿām) is made masculine in His statement ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾ [Surah al-Nahl 16:66], and then it is made feminine afterward in His statement ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [Surah al-Muʾminun 23:22; Surah Ghafir 40:80].

Whoever reads ﴿yusqā﴾ with a ya' makes "grapevines" something that may be masculine or feminine, like "livestock."

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: whoever reads ﴿tusqā﴾ has in mind the feminine gender of "the crops, the gardens, and the palm trees," and whoever makes it masculine has in mind that all of them are watered with one water, while their produce differs: sour and sweet. In this there is a sign. [[This is the statement of al-Farra' in Maʿani al-Qur'an, in his explanation of the verse.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: The more preferred of the two readings to me, to recite with, is the reading of the one who reads it with a ta': ﴿tuqsā bi-māʾin wāḥid﴾, on the basis that its meaning is: the gardens, the palm trees, and the crops are watered with one water, because ﴿tusqā﴾ comes after their mention has already preceded, and they are a collective noun for non-human beings. The other reading is not impossible in meaning: that is, all of that is watered with one water, sweet water, not brackish.

* *

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: These are two widely transmitted readings with one meaning. Whichever of them the reciter reads is correct. However, the ya' is more preferred by me in recitation, because it is in the context of a speech that begins with ﴿God is He who raised the heavens﴾; so reading it with a ya' is more appropriate, since that is the case.

* *

The meaning of the speech is: the gardens of grapevines, crops, and palm trees, both clustered and non-clustered, are watered with one water, sweet and not salty, and God differentiates among their flavors, favoring some of them over others in taste: this one is sweet, and this one is sour.

Al-Nasa'i said: "Weak, abandoned, and not trustworthy." He is mentioned in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/173, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/277, and Mizan al-iʿtidal 1:438. This report was narrated by al-Tirmidhi also, from Mahmud ibn Khidash, with this same chain and wording, in the explanation of the verse. Then he said: "This is a good, strange hadith, and Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah narrated it (the following chain) from al-Aʿmash, similar to this. Sayf ibn Muhammad is the brother of ʿAmmar ibn Muhammad, and ʿAmmar is more reliable than him, and he is the nephew of Sufyan al-Thawri." So it is strange that al-Tirmidhi would deem a chain good that contains this liar, Sayf ibn Muhammad. See the takhrij of the following report. In the printed edition it read: "Sayf ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad narrated to us, from Sufyan al-Thawri," which its publisher erred in, since he did not study the chain, and he altered what is in the manuscript. In the manuscript it read: "Sayf ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad Sufyan al-Thawri," with a mark of doubt and hesitation in the margin. Its correct form is what has been recorded here. See the explanation of "al-Farsi" as passed on page 343, footnote 2.]]

20127. Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhi narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Raqqi narrated to us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUmar al-Raqqi narrated to us, from Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding His statement ﴿and We favor some of them over others in produce﴾: "The daqal, the Farsi, the sweet, and the sour." [[Report 20127: "Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhi," the teacher of al-Tabari, was one of the vessels of hadith, trustworthy, and has passed many times, the last being number 19876. "Sulayman ibn ʿUbayd Allah al-Ansari al-Raqqi," "Abu Ayyub al-Hattab," Ibn Abi Hatim said: truthful. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. Al-Nasa'i said: "Not strong." Ibn Maʿin said: "Nothing." Al-Bukhari mentioned no criticism of him. He is in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/26, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/127, and Mizan al-iʿtidal 1:418. "ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAmr al-Raqqi" is trustworthy, narrated from by the group, and has passed many times, the last being number 16945. "Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah al-Jazari" is trustworthy, narrated from by the group, and has passed many times, the last being number 16945. This report was pointed to by al-Tirmidhi, as I mentioned in the previous footnote. Al-Dhahabi also mentioned it in Mizan al-iʿtidal 1:418, in the biography of "Sulayman ibn ʿUbayd Allah," with this chain complete. Then he said: "Al-ʿUqayli said: No one narrated it except Sulayman, and it is only known through Sayf ibn Muhammad from al-Aʿmash." I say: Sayf is perished. So this chain, as you see, contains destruction, and the weak narrator's sole transmission of it is problematic. How then was it permissible for al-Tirmidhi to deem it good with these defects that taint it from every side? (See ʿIlal al-Hadith by Ibn Abi Hatim 2:80, number 1723.) See the explanation of "al-Farsi" as passed on page 343, footnote 2.]]

* *

As for His statement ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason﴾: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, in God's difference among these clusters of adjacent lands and their fruits and crops, as we have described and explained, [there is] clear evidence and a lesson for a people who reason about this difference: that the One who differentiated them in this manner is the One who differentiates among His creatures in what He allots them of guidance and misguidance, success and abandonment. He grants success to this one and abandons that one, guides this one and misguides that one. Had He willed, He would have made them all equal, just as, had He willed, He would have made equal the eating of the fruits of Paradise, which are drunk as one drink and watered with one watering, yet they differ in what is eaten.

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: 'When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?' Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; those will have shackles around their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally" (13:5).

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says: "And if you are amazed" – O Muhammad – at these polytheists who take as gods, to be worshipped besides Him, things that neither harm nor benefit – then amazing is their saying, "When we are dust" and have decayed and been annihilated, "will we indeed be in a new creation?" – meaning, will we indeed be recreated and brought back as a new creation, as we were before our deaths? – denying God's power and rejecting reward, punishment and resurrection after death. As related:

20128. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying" – if you are amazed, O Muhammad – "then amazing is their saying, 'When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?'" – the Merciful, Blessed and Exalted, is amazed at their denial of resurrection after death.

20129. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying" – he said: If you are amazed at their denial, while they have seen of God's power and His command, and what examples He has set for them, and He showed them the life of the dead in the dead earth – if you are amazed at these, then be amazed at their saying, "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Do they not see that We created them from a drop of semen? Is creation from semen harder, or creation from dust and bones? [Note on the isnad: in the printed edition alone, in place of "Ibn Wahb" it reads "Ibrahim", and I do not know where this came from; it is a recurring chain in the tafsir.]

* *

Scholars of Arabic differed concerning the reason for repeating the interrogative in His words "will we indeed be in a new creation?", after the first interrogative in His words "When we are dust?"

Some grammarians of Basra said: The first (idha) is an adverb of time, and the second is the element upon which the interrogation falls, as you say: "Is Friday the day that Zayd is departing?" He said: Whoever places a second interrogative upon His words "When we are dust" makes it an adverb of time attached to something mentioned before it, as if they had been told, "You will be resurrected," and they said, "When we are dust?" and then he made this a second interrogative. He said: This is remote. He said: If you wish, you do not make "idha" in your statement an interrogative, and you make the interrogation in wording fall on "a-innā" (will we indeed), as if you said: "Is Friday, is God's servant departing?" and you suppress its negation. This is the position of what you began with "idha"; and it is not common in speech if you said, "Today, indeed Abdullah is departing," it would not be well-formed, though it is permissible; and the Arabs have said, "I did not know that he is righteous," meaning, "he is righteous as far as I know."

[Editorial note: This passage of al-Tabari's commentary requires clarification, as he has expressed the matter in an obscure way, so that the editor of the first edition felt compelled to correct and alter what he altered, due to the obscurity of what Abu Ja'far wrote here. This is why I departed from my earlier practice of not commenting on the grammatical matters in the tafsir. I fear that some part of the speech may have dropped out.

Abu Ja'far's speech in this paragraph intends to explain the repetition of the interrogative, as he mentioned in the heading on the disagreement of the people of Arabic, but he implied the speech by way of implication, and this is its explanation and elaboration.

1. His words: "Some grammarians of Basra said: The first is an adverb. The second is that upon which the interrogation falls, as you say: 'Is Friday the day that Zayd is departing?'"
He means that "idha" is an adverb, attached to an omitted element after it indicated by His words "will we indeed be in a new creation," which is "resurrected"; as if he said, "When we are dust, will we be resurrected?" So the adverb "idha" is attached to the omitted "resurrected," and the meaning is: "Will we be resurrected when we are dust?" This is like your saying, "Is Friday the day Zayd departs?" meaning "Does Zayd depart on Friday?" The interrogation falls in the first on "resurrected" and in the other example on "Zayd departs." This is the interpretation of the grammarians of Basra, as found in the books of tafsir.

2. Then he said after it: "Whoever places a second interrogative upon His words 'When we are dust,' makes it an adverb attached to something mentioned before it, as if they had been told, 'You will be resurrected?' and they said, 'When we are dust?' and then he made this a second interrogative. He said: This is remote."
He means that "idha," the adverb, is attached to an element before it, which is what they were told, "You will be resurrected," and they said, "When we are dust?" The interrogation here falls on "idha," that is, on the adverb. This is considered remote, because it brings an omitted element before the adverb for which there is no evidence in the speech.

3. Then he said: "He said: If you wish, you do not make 'idha' an interrogative, and you make the interrogation in wording fall on 'a-innā,' as if you said, 'Is Friday, is God's servant departing?' and you suppress its negation. This is the position of what you began with 'idha,' and it is not common in speech."
He means that the first interrogative is a superfluous addition on "idha," and you suppress its negation, so you repeated the interrogative, as you repeated it in your saying, "Is Friday, is God's servant departing?" This repetition is not common in speech.

4. Then he said: "If you said, 'Today, indeed Abdullah is departing,' it would not be well-formed, though it is permissible. The Arabs have said, 'I did not know that he is righteous,' meaning, 'he is righteous as far as I know.'"
He means that this fourth form is not well-formed, though permissible, because it requires that "idha" then be an adverb attached to His words "in a new creation," that is, to the predicate of "inna," and the predicate of "inna" does not precede it; so it is even more so that what the predicate governs does not precede it. That is why your saying "Today, indeed Abdullah is departing" is not well-formed, because "today" is governed by "departing," which is the predicate of "inna," so placing it before "inna" is not well-formed, though permissible, since what follows "inna" does not govern what precedes it. He cited its permissibility by the Arabic saying, "I did not know that he is righteous," where "ma" here is temporal, meaning "in my knowledge, or during my knowledge," and the Arabs placed "ma 'alimtu" before "inna," meaning "he is righteous as far as I know." This clarification, which I have expanded upon to explain Abu Ja'far's statement, I have not found anyone among the authors of tafsir books or the books on the grammar of the Qur'an who addressed it as Abu Ja'far did in his clarification. They all passed over it and summarized it, and did not explain it as Abu Ja'far did. Abu Hayyan, who is what he is in tracing the sayings of the grammarians and in investigating al-Tabari's statement in his tafsir, also omitted its explanation and passed over it, due to the obscurity of Abu Ja'far's expression in this place. So I hope I have reached a satisfactory level in explaining it, God willing.]

* *

Others said: "Idha" is a conditional (jaza'), not a time-adverb ("waqt"), and what follows it is its answer, when there is no interrogative in the second part, and the meaning belongs to it, since it is what is sought. He said: Do you not see that you say, "If you stand, will Zayd stand, or will he stand?" – whoever apocopates (jazm) does so because it has come in the position of the answer to the condition, and whoever raises (raf') does so because the interrogation belongs to it. He cited the verse of the poet:

"I swore to him: if you travel by night, there will not cease to be ahead of you a house of mine, traveling."

So he apocopated the answer of the oath because it came in the position of the answer to the condition, though the correct form is the raised one. He said: So it is with this verse. He said: Whoever repeats the interrogative, does so because it is what is relied upon, and leaves the first part.

* *

As for His words: "Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord" – exalted is He, says: those who denied resurrection and rejected reward and punishment and said, "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" – they are those who denied the power of their Lord and disbelieved His messenger, and they are those who have shackles on their necks on the Day of Resurrection in the Fire of Hell. [See the explanation of "shackles" above, 13:168; he did not clarify it here or there adequately, as is his habit.] "Those are the companions of the Fire" – he says: they are the inhabitants of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection; "they will abide therein eternally" – he says: they will remain there forever, neither dying therein nor leaving it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 6:

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them. Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ (6)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿They ask you to hasten﴾ O Muhammad, [[See the explanation of "al-isti'jal" (hastening) above at 15, 33, 101.]] the polytheists of your people, to receive calamity and punishment before well-being and safety, saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 32]. And they know what befell those nations before them that disobeyed their Lord and denied their messengers, of the punishments of Allah and His great afflictions, [[See the explanation of "khala" (to pass away) above at 12:415, note 4, and the references there.]] from among a nation that was transformed into apes and another into swine, and a nation destroyed by the earthquake, and another by the sinking of the earth. These are the ﴿exemplary punishments﴾ of which Allah, may His praise be exalted, spoke: ﴿and exemplary punishments have already passed before them.﴾

And al-mathulat (the exemplary punishments) are the punishments that cause dread. Its singular is "mathulah," with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', and it is pluralized as "mathulat," just as the singular of "al-sadaqat" is "sadaqah," and its plural is "sadaqat." [[As-sadaqah means a woman's dower. It has already passed in Surah al-Nisa', verse 4, at 7:552, though it was not fully explained there.]] It is reported that Tamim among the Arabs vowel both the mim and the tha' of "al-muthulat," so its singular in their dialect is "muthlah," pluralized as "muthulat," like "ghurfah" and "ghurufat." The verb from it is "mathaltu bihi amthulu mathlan," with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the tha'. When you want to say that you inflicted retribution on someone for another, you say "amthaltuhu min sahibihi umthiluhu imthalan," meaning that you exacted retribution from him.

* *

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿and exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾, the events of Allah among the nations of those who passed before you. And His words: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾, the polytheists of the Arabs hastened for evil before good, and they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾.

20131. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾, he said: for the punishment before the well-being. ﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾, he said: the punishments.

20132. al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Shababah narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿al-mathulat﴾, he said: the parables.

20133. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid=

20134. And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

20135. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿and exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾, he said: ﴿al-mathulat﴾ is what Allah made an example of the nations by the punishment with which He punished them. The exemplary punishments of torment passed, and they had already occurred before them, and they knew of that, and what Allah made an example of them reached them when they disobeyed Him and disobeyed His messengers. [[In the printed edition: "mathal Allah fi al-umam" (the example Allah made among the nations); I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]]

* *

As for His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed your Lord, O Muhammad, is full of concealment of the sins of those among mankind who repent of their sins, leaving off disgracing them for them on the Day of Standing, and pardoning them for their punishment for them, both in this world and the next. ﴿Despite their wrongdoing﴾ means: despite their doing what they did of that without My permission for them to do it. ﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever perishes persisting in his disobedience on the Day of Resurrection, if He does not hasten that for him in this world, or combine both for him in this world and the Hereafter.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This statement, although its outward form is that of a report, is in fact a warning from Allah and a threat to the polytheists of the people of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), should they not turn back and repent of their disbelief before the descent of Allah's vengeance upon them.

* *

20137. Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind﴾, he said: but your Lord.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 7:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people is a guide﴾ (7)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, mentioning: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ O Muhammad, from among your people= ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾ Why has a sign from his Lord not been sent down upon Muhammad? [[See the explanation of "lawla" (why not) previously, 15:205, note (1), and the references there, then 15:210.]] They mean a sign and proof for him of his prophethood [[See the explanation of the verse previously in the index of language (abā).]] This is like their saying: ﴿Why has not a treasure been sent down upon him, or an angel come with him?﴾ [Surah Hud: 12]. God says to him: O Muhammad, ﴿you are only a warner﴾ to them, warning them of God's punishment lest it descend upon them for their polytheism [[See the explanation of "al-indhar" (warning) previously in the index of language, n-dh-r.]]. ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾. He says: and for every people there is an imam whom they follow, and a guide who goes before them, guiding them either to good or to evil.

* *

It derives from "hadi al-faras" (the horse's neck), which guides the rest of its body. [[See the explanation of "al-hadi" previously, 2:293.]]

* *

In accordance with what we have said, the people of interpretation have spoken, though they differ regarding who is meant by the guide in this place.

Some of them said: He is the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Those who said that:

God said: ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people is a guide﴾, for every people there is a caller who calls them to God.

20139- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi,

from Ikrimah= and Mansur, from Abu al-Duha: ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people is a guide﴾. Both said: Muhammad is the "warner" and he is the "guide".

20140- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Ikrimah, the like of it.

20141- al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from his father, from Ikrimah, the like of it.

Others said: its meaning is: for every people there is a caller.

Those who said that:

20162- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾. He said: a caller.

* *

I have already clarified the meaning of "guidance", and that it is the followed leader who goes before the people. [[See what preceded, p. 353.]] Given that this is so, it is permissible that it refers to God, who guides His creation, and His creation follows His guidance and adheres to His command and prohibition.

It is also permissible that it refers to the Prophet of God whom his community follows.

It is also permissible that it refers to an imam among the imams who is followed, and whose method and path his companions follow.

It is also permissible that it refers to a caller among the callers to good or to evil.

Given that this is so, there is no statement more correct in this matter than to say, as He, mighty is His praise, said: Muhammad is the warner to whom the warning was sent, and for every people there is a guide who guides them, and they follow him and adhere to him.

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs lose and what they gain, and everything with Him is in measure﴾ (8).

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ They deny God's power to restore them to a new creation after their annihilation and decay, while they do not deny His power to originate them and fashion them in the wombs, and to direct and transform them there from state to state. So He begins the report about that from its beginning, and its meaning is what I have described. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "ما وصف" (what he described); the correct reading is what I have written.]] So He, majestic is His praise, says: ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs lose and what they gain.﴾ That is: what the wombs lose of their load within the nine months by discharging menstrual blood [[See the explanation of "al-ghayd" (what is lost) above, 15: 334 and following.]], and ﴿what they gain﴾ in their load beyond the nine months, to make up for what was lost of the load within the nine months through the discharge of menstrual blood. ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾: nothing exceeds its measure from its decree, and no matter that He has willed and ordained is shortened from its ordinance, just as the load of a female does not increase beyond what has been decreed for it, nor fall short of the limit set for it.

* *

"Al-miqdar" (measure) is a form of "al-qadar" (decree).

And His saying: ﴿and everything with Him is in measure.﴾

20201. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, His saying: ﴿and everything with Him is in measure﴾: yes, by God, He has preserved for them their provision and their terms, and has made for them a known appointed time.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Most High﴾ (13:9)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says: God knows what is hidden from you and from your sight, so that you do not see it, and what you do see and perceive with your eyes. Nothing is concealed from Him, because they are His creation [[See the explanation of "the unseen and the witnessed" in what has preceded, 11:464–465.]] and under His management. "The Great" is the One before whom everything is lesser [[See the explanation of "the Great" in what has preceded, 8:318.]]. "The Most High" is the One who rises above everything by His power.

It is *al-mutaʿāl* (the Most High) from *al-ʿuluww* (height), in the pattern of *al-mutaqārib* (the near) from *al-qurb* (nearness) and *al-mutadānī* (the close) from *al-dunuww* (closeness). [[See also the explanation of "al-taʿālī" in what has preceded, 15:47, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿It is alike to Him whether one of you speaks secretly or speaks openly, and whether he is hidden by night or goes forth freely by day﴾ (13:10)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says: equal in the sight of God, O people, is the one among you who speaks secretly, and the one who speaks aloud, and the one who is hidden by night in its darkness through disobedience to God. "And goes forth freely by day" means: he who appears openly by day in its light. None of that is hidden from Him. Their secret and their open conduct are alike to Him, since nothing is concealed or hidden from Him. [[See the explanation of "secrecy" in what has preceded, p. 198, note 1, and the references there.]] [[See the explanation of "loudness" in what has preceded, 9:343–349, 358; 11:368; 13:353, note 4, and the references there.]]

* *

It is said of it: *sariba yasribu surūban*, meaning he appeared openly, as Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

*Annā sarayti wa-kunti ghayra sarūb*
*wa-tuqarribu al-aḥlāmu ghayra qarīb* [[His Diwan, p. 5; al-Lisan (s-r-b) and many others. It is also transmitted as "sarabti" with a bāʾ, and his words "ghayr sarūb" mean "not distant in your course," or as Abu Ja'far said in his commentary below.]]

That is: "How did you travel by night [across] the distance of this road, and you did not come out and show yourself?" [[The addition in parentheses is necessary to make the meaning of the sentence correct.]]

Some of them said: *al-sārib* is the one who goes in his *sarb*, that is, in his course and place. [[I think he means Abu ʿUbayda in *Majaz al-Qur'an* 1:323, but his wording is: "going in his *sarb*, that is, his paths and aspects," which is better than what is in the *tafsir*, and I fear it may be a copyist's error or slip.]]

The scholars of the Arabic language differed concerning *al-sarb*.

Some of them said: "He is safe in his *sarb*," with the *sīn* vowelled with a fatḥa.

Others said: "He is safe in his *sirb*," with the *sīn* vowelled with a kasra.

The *man* in His saying: ﴿whether one of you speaks secretly, or speaks openly, or whoever is hidden by night﴾ — the first of these is in the nominative (*raf'*) by His saying *sawā'* ("alike"). The second is conjoined (*maʿṭūfa*) to the first, and the third to the second.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Most High﴾ (13:9)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says: God knows what is hidden from you and from your sight, so that you do not see it, and what you do see and perceive with your eyes. Nothing is concealed from Him, because they are His creation [[See the explanation of "the unseen and the witnessed" in what has preceded, 11:464–465.]] and under His management. "The Great" is the One before whom everything is lesser [[See the explanation of "the Great" in what has preceded, 8:318.]]. "The Most High" is the One who rises above everything by His power.

It is *al-mutaʿāl* (the Most High) from *al-ʿuluww* (height), in the pattern of *al-mutaqārib* (the near) from *al-qurb* (nearness) and *al-mutadānī* (the close) from *al-dunuww* (closeness). [[See also the explanation of "al-taʿālī" in what has preceded, 15:47, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿It is alike to Him whether one of you speaks secretly or speaks openly, and whether he is hidden by night or goes forth freely by day﴾ (13:10)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says: equal in the sight of God, O people, is the one among you who speaks secretly, and the one who speaks aloud, and the one who is hidden by night in its darkness through disobedience to God. "And goes forth freely by day" means: he who appears openly by day in its light. None of that is hidden from Him. Their secret and their open conduct are alike to Him, since nothing is concealed or hidden from Him. [[See the explanation of "secrecy" in what has preceded, p. 198, note 1, and the references there.]] [[See the explanation of "loudness" in what has preceded, 9:343–349, 358; 11:368; 13:353, note 4, and the references there.]]

* *

It is said of it: *sariba yasribu surūban*, meaning he appeared openly, as Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

*Annā sarayti wa-kunti ghayra sarūb*
*wa-tuqarribu al-aḥlāmu ghayra qarīb* [[His Diwan, p. 5; al-Lisan (s-r-b) and many others. It is also transmitted as "sarabti" with a bāʾ, and his words "ghayr sarūb" mean "not distant in your course," or as Abu Ja'far said in his commentary below.]]

That is: "How did you travel by night [across] the distance of this road, and you did not come out and show yourself?" [[The addition in parentheses is necessary to make the meaning of the sentence correct.]]

Some of them said: *al-sārib* is the one who goes in his *sarb*, that is, in his course and place. [[I think he means Abu ʿUbayda in *Majaz al-Qur'an* 1:323, but his wording is: "going in his *sarb*, that is, his paths and aspects," which is better than what is in the *tafsir*, and I fear it may be a copyist's error or slip.]]

The scholars of the Arabic language differed concerning *al-sarb*.

Some of them said: "He is safe in his *sarb*," with the *sīn* vowelled with a fatḥa.

Others said: "He is safe in his *sirb*," with the *sīn* vowelled with a kasra.

* *

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) said what we have said on this matter.

**Those who said that:**

He said: "He is the person of doubtful conduct, hidden by night. When he goes out by day, he shows people that he is free of sin."

His saying: ﴿and whether he is hidden by night or goes forth freely by day﴾, that is, in the darkness of the night. "*Sārib*" means: openly by day.

* *

The *man* in His saying: ﴿whether one of you speaks secretly, or speaks openly, or whoever is hidden by night﴾ — the first of these is in the nominative (*raf'*) by His saying *sawā'* ("alike"). The second is conjoined (*maʿṭūfa*) to the first, and the third to the second.

**The explanation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿For him there are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of God. Indeed, God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when God wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no guardian other than Him.﴾ (13:11)**

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of *ta'wil* (interpretation of the Qur'an) differed concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: Its meaning is that for God, may His remembrance be exalted, there are *mu'aqqibat* (successive ones). They said: The pronoun in His words *lahu* ("for him") refers to the name of God. The *mu'aqqibat* are those who follow one another over the servant. That is because the angels of the night, when they ascend at daytime, are followed by the angels of the day, and when the day ends, the angels of the day ascend and are followed by the angels of the night. They said: It is said *mu'aqqibat*, and *al-mala'ika* (the angels) is the plural of *malak* (angel), which is masculine and not feminine. The singular of *al-mala'ika* is *mu'aqqib*, and its plural is *mu'aqqiba*. Then the plural of the plural was formed, meaning the plural of *mu'aqqib* after the plural of *mu'aqqiba* had been formed, and it was said *mu'aqqibat*, just as it is said *sadat Sa'd* ("the lords of Sa'd") and *rijalat Bani Fulan* ("the men of the sons of So-and-so"), the plural of *rajul* (man).

* * *

As for His words, ﴿from before him and from behind him﴾, by His words ﴿from before him﴾ is meant: from the front of this one who hides himself by night and goes about freely by day. ﴿And from behind him﴾: from behind his back.

Mention of those who said this:

20210 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Mansur, meaning Ibn Zadhan, from al-Hasan, concerning this verse, ﴿for him there are successive ones before him and behind him﴾, he said: "The angels."

20211 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Salam ibn Salih al-Qushayri narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Jarir narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, from Kinana al-Adawi, who said: Uthman ibn Affan entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, inform me about the servant: how many angels are with him?" He said: "There is an angel on your right, over your good deeds, and he is a trustworthy overseer of the one on the left. When you do a good deed, it is recorded as ten. When you do an evil deed, the one on the left says to the one on the right: 'Write!' He says: 'No, perhaps he will seek God's forgiveness and repent!' When he says it three times, he says: 'Yes, write it, may God relieve us of him! How evil a companion he is, how little he watches over [his duty to] God, and how little he is ashamed before us!' God says: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is an observer with him, ready﴾ (Surah Qaf: 18). And there are two angels, before you and behind you; God says: ﴿for him there are successive ones before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of God﴾. And there is an angel holding your forelock: if you humble yourself before God, He raises you, and if you act arrogantly toward God, He breaks you. And there are two angels on your lips, who guard over you only the sending of blessings upon Muhammad. And there is an angel standing over your mouth, who does not let a snake enter your mouth. And there are two angels over your eyes. These are ten angels over every son of Adam, and the angels of the night descend upon the angels of the day [because the angels of the night are other than the angels of the day]. So these are twenty angels over every son of Adam, and Iblis (is) by day and his offspring by night."

[Footnote: This is a chain of narration similar to one already passed, Nos. 1386 and 1395. It is a problematic and objectionable chain. "Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Salam ibn Salih al-Qushayri" — earlier it was "al-Tustari," and in that place in Ibn Kathir it is "al-Qushayri." We do not know which is correct, and we have not found any mention of him in any of the books of biographical evaluation. As for "Ali ibn Jarir," we do not know who he is either, as we said earlier, but I add that Ibn Abi Hatim recorded in *al-Jarh wa'l-Ta'dil*: "Ali ibn Jarir al-Barudi, he narrated from him… My father was asked about Ali ibn Jarir al-Barudi, and he said: *saduq* (truthful)." I do not think he is the one in our chain; this appears to be a later figure. (Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/178.) As for Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far, he is trustworthy (*thiqa*), mentioned earlier under No. 1386. As for Kinana al-Adawi, he is Kinana ibn Nu'aym al-Adawi, a trustworthy Successor (*tabi'i*), but it is not mentioned that he met Uthman ibn Affan or narrated from him. So this is a hadith with strangeness (*nakara*) and severe weakness, and Abu Ja'far al-Tabari alone narrated it from al-Muthanna. See Ibn Kathir's *Tafsir* 4:503, and *al-Durr al-Manthur* 4:48. Ibn Kathir said: it is a very strange hadith.]

Others said: Rather, by *al-mu'aqqibat* in this place is meant the guards who follow one another around the ruler (*al-amir*).

Mention of those who said this:

[Footnote: In the printed edition: "the one guarded from the command of God," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two interpretations in this matter is the view of the one who said that the pronoun in His words, ﴿for him (*lahu*) there are successive ones﴾, refers to "the one" (*man*) in His words, ﴿and the one who hides himself by night﴾, and that the *mu'aqqibat* before him and behind him are his guards and his *jalawiza* (enforcers), [Footnote: *Jalawiza* is the plural of *jalawaz* (with a kasra on the jim and sukun on the lam), the policeman who walks before the ruler and carries out his orders], just as those whose statements we have mentioned said.

We said that this is the more correct of the two interpretations because His words, ﴿for him there are successive ones﴾, are closer to His words, ﴿and the one who hides himself by night﴾, than to the Knower of the unseen. So because of its nearness to it, it is more appropriate that they be of his mention, and that this be what is intended, together with the indication of the words of God, ﴿And when God wills misfortune for a people, there is no repelling it﴾, that they are the ones intended by that.

That is because He, may His praise be exalted, mentioned a people who are disobedient to Him and people of doubt, who hide themselves by night and appear by day, and who protect themselves in their own estimation by guards who guard them and a defense that prevents them from the people of His obedience from coming between them and what they do of disobedience to God. Then He informed that when God, may His remembrance be exalted, wills misfortune for them, their guards will not benefit them, and their protection will not ward off anything from them.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿guarding him by the command of God﴾, the scholars of *ta'wil* differed concerning the interpretation of this phrase in the same way as they differed concerning the interpretation of His words, ﴿for him there are successive ones﴾.

So whoever said that the *mu'aqqibat* are the angels said that those who guard him by the command of God are also the angels.

And whoever said that the *mu'aqqibat* are the guards and enforcers from among the sons of Adam said that those who guard him by the command of God are those guards.

* * *

They also differed concerning the meaning of His words, ﴿by the command of God﴾.

Some of them said: Their guarding him is from His command.

Others said: ﴿guarding him by the command of God﴾ means "by the command of God."

Mention of those who said: those who guard him are the angels, and who directed His words, ﴿by the command of God﴾ to the meaning that their guarding him is from the command of God:
