Others said: the meaning of that is: they guard him from the command of God, and "the command of God" is the jinn, and those who seek to harm him and do him injury before the decree of God comes. When His decree comes, they leave him to it.
Mention of those who said this:
20244. Abu Hurayra al-Dubai'i related to me, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Mansur, from Talhah, from Ibrahim, regarding ﴿they guard him from the command of God﴾: he said, "From the jinn." [[The report 20244: "Abu Hurayra al-Dubai'i" was mentioned in the previous report. And "Abu Dawud" is al-Tayalisi.]]
20245. Siwar ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, saying: I heard Layth narrating, from Mujahid, that he said: "There is no servant but that he has an angel assigned to guard him in his sleep and his waking, from the jinn, the humans and the vermin. None of them comes to him intending him harm but it says, 'Behind you!' except for something God has permitted, which then strikes him."
20246. al-Hasan ibn 'Arafa narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Alhani, from Yazid ibn Shurayh, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: "If every plain and every mountain were to be revealed to the son of Adam, he would see devils upon every thing of that. Were it not that God has assigned to you angels who ward off from you in your eating, your drinking and your private parts, you would then be snatched away."
20247. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, saying: 'Umarah ibn Abi Hafsa narrated to us, from Abu Mijlaz, who said: A man from Murad came to 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, while he was praying, and said: "Be on your guard, for some people from Murad intend to kill you!" He said: "With every man are two angels who guard him from what has not been decreed. When the decree comes, they leave him to it. Indeed, the appointed term is a strong shield."
20248. al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Dhakwan, from Abu Ghalib, from Abu Umama, who said: "There is no human but that with him is an assigned angel who wards off from him until he hands him over to that which was decreed for him."
* *
Others said: the meaning of that is: they guard over him from God.
Mention of those who said this:
20249. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding ﴿they guard him from the command of God﴾: he said, "They guard over him from God."
* *
Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Ibn Jurayj, by his statement "they guard over him," means the angels assigned to the son of Adam, guarding his good deeds and his bad deeds, and they are the "mu'aqqibat" in our view. They record for the son of Adam his good deeds and his bad deeds by the command of God.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: According to this view, it must be that the meaning of His statement ﴿from the command of God﴾ is that the guardians are by the command of God, or they guard by the command of God. And the "hu" (his) in His statement ﴿they guard him﴾ must be taken as singular and masculine, although what is intended by it is the good deeds and bad deeds, because it is a reference back to the mention of "man," who is hidden by night and goes freely by day. And the one "hidden by night" is mentioned in place of the report about his bad and good deeds, as is said in ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 82].
'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd used to say, concerning this, something other than all these views:
20250. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement ﴿and whoever is hidden by night and goes freely by day﴾: "'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a came to the Messenger of God ﷺ." ["Arbad ibn Rabi'a" is how it came here from Ibn Zayd, and likewise it came from Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Qurashi in what Ibn Sa'd related from him in his Tabaqat, 1/2/51. And "Arbad" is: "Arbad ibn Qays ibn Juz' ibn Khalid ibn Ja'far ibn Kilab," and he was the maternal half-brother of Labid, and "Labid" is "Labid ibn Rabi'a ibn Malik ibn Ja'far ibn Kilab." It seems that Ibn Zayd and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Qurashi said "Arbad ibn Rabi'a" because of his being the brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a. I do not know how they said this, nor why they said it. I have not found it in any place other than these two. See the book "Jawami' al-Sira" by Ibn Hazm, p. 12, note 1.]] 'Amir said: "What will you give me if I follow you?" He said: "You are a horseman; I will give you the reins of horses." He said: "No." He said: "Then what do you seek?" He said: "For me the East, and for you the West." He said: "No." He said: "Then for me the wilderness, and for you the settled lands." He said: "No. I will fill it against you with horses and men." He said: "God will prevent you from that, and the two sons of Qaylah" [In the printed edition: "and the sons of Qaylah," but the correct reading is what is in the manuscript, in the dual. "Qaylah" is the mother of the Aws and the Khazraj.] — meaning the Aws and the Khazraj.
He said: So they both went out. 'Amir said to Arbad: "If that man is ours to be overcome, if we killed him, not two goats would butt heads over him, and they would be content for us to pay blood-money to them, and they would love peace and hate war when they see that a matter has happened." The other said: "If you wish, let us consult one another." And he said: "Go back, and I will occupy him away from you with argument, and you be behind him and strike him with the sword in one blow." So they were as such: one behind the Prophet ﷺ, and the other said: "Recount to us your tales." He said: "What do you say?" He said: "Your Qur'an!" [In the printed edition: "He said, what does your Qur'an say," with the word "he said" removed from the text; I have restored what is in the manuscript, meaning: "Recite to me your Qur'an."] So he went on disputing with him and making him wait, until he said: "What is wrong with you, have you been unnerved?" [Between this and what follows there is confusion in the text, and I fear there may be a gap or omission; the context shows that he began to argue with the Messenger of God ﷺ, and looked at Arbad, making him wait. When they departed, 'Amir said to Arbad: "What is wrong with you, have you been unnerved?"]
He said: "I placed my hand on the hilt of my sword, [and it stiffened], so that I could neither draw it nor move it, nor move it at all." [The insertion between brackets was added by the first editor from al-Durr al-Manthur.] He said: So they both went out, and when they were at al-Harra, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr heard of that, so they went out to them, each of them in his armour, with his spear in his hand, and girt with his sword. They said to 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl: "O one-eyed [and a mess], O you of the white patch [or: O bald one]! Are you the one who makes conditions with the Messenger of God ﷺ? Were it not that you are under the protection of the Messenger of God ﷺ, you would not have left the dwelling until we struck your neck, but [we do not seek help]." [In the printed edition: "O one-eyed, O wicked one, O spotted one," which differs from the manuscript. The manuscript reads: "ناعور حسما يا أبلخ," and I was unable to find the report elsewhere to correct it, and I have been unable to uncover the distortion in it, so I have recorded it as it is. "Al-Ablakh" is one who is great in himself, bold in committing wrongdoing.] [In the printed edition: "tashtariṭ," and I have recorded what is in the manuscript.] [In the printed edition: "ḍarabt," and I have recorded what is in the manuscript.] [This is another word which I have recorded as it is in the manuscript, undotted, and I did not come to know how to read it; but the printer of the printed edition made it "lā tastabqīn," dotting it, so it became meaningless. As for al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur, he omitted it as is his custom, and was relieved of its difficulty.] The one who was more hostile to him of the two men was Usayd ibn al-Hudayr, [so he said: "Who is this?" They said: "Usayd ibn Hudayr"]? [This addition is necessary; I have recorded it from al-Durr al-Manthur.] He said: "If his father were alive, he would not have done this to me!" Then he said to Arbad: "Go out, you, O Arbad, toward the region of 'Adana," [In the printed edition: "ila 'Dhiyya," and there is no place in the lands of the Arabs by this name; what is in the manuscript is "'Adana" (with an 'ayn and dal vowelled), and it is land belonging to the Banu Fazara, to the north of al-Sharba. Al-Asma'i said in defining Najd: "The Wadi al-Rimma cuts between 'Adana and al-Sharba. If you cross the Rimma heading east, you take up al-Sharba, and if you cross the Rimma toward the north, you take up 'Adana." I hope what I have read is the correct one.] "and I will go out to Najd, then we will gather the men and meet against him." So Arbad went out until, when he was at al-Raqam, [al-Raqam, it is clear that it is a place; see Mu'jam al-Buldan, Mu'jam ma Ista'jam, and Sifat Jazirat al-'Arab of al-Hamdani: 176, but I am in doubt about all of this], God sent a cloud of summer in which was a thunderbolt! It burned him. He said: 'Amir went out until, when he was in a valley called al-Jarir, God sent the plague upon him, and he began to cry out: "O family of 'Amir! A boil like the boil of the young camel is killing me! O family of 'Amir, a boil like the boil of the young camel is killing me, and death too in the house of a Sulayliyya!" She was a woman from Qays. That is the saying of God: ﴿It is the same whether any of you conceal speech or speak it aloud﴾, and he recited until he reached: ﴿they guard him﴾, "those guardians from the command of God." This is precedence and sequence for the Messenger of God ﷺ: ﴿guardians who guard him from before him and behind him, those are guardians by the command of God.﴾ And He said to these two: ﴿Indeed God does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves﴾, and he recited until he reached: ﴿He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾, the verse, and he recited until he reached: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾
He said: Labid recited, concerning his brother Arbad, weeping over him:
I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rising of al-Simak and al-Asad [the star-mansions],
[Diwan, poem no. 5, lines 2, 3; they will recur on p. 394; and before the two lines, which is its beginning: "What the Vicissitude leaves no one bereft, neither a compassionate father nor a son."
And "al-Hutuf" are the appointed terms of death. And his saying "the rising of al-Simak and al-Asad": he means al-Simak al-A'zal, whose rising is four nights in Tishrin al-Awwal (the month of October), and it is a heavy rising. As for "al-Asad," he means "Zubrat al-Asad," whose rising is four nights in late Ab (the month of August), and in the rising of Zubra there is heavy rain (see the book al-Anwa' of Ibn Qutayba, pp. 58, 59 / 64, 65). And all of that is in the season of summer.
Labid says: I used to fear for him every death I knew, except this sudden death from the summer thunderbolts.
And his saying "the time has afflicted me," that is, it brought upon me the painful calamity and the grievous misfortune. "The day of distress" is the day of hardship in war, when souls dislike death. And "al-Najd" (with a fatha, then a damma) is the courageous, strong one of great valour, quick to respond to what he is called to, whether good or evil, with a steadfastness in what others are unable to do.]
The thunder and the thunderbolts have afflicted me with the horseman, on the day of distress, the brave one.
[The report 20250: al-Suyuti related it in al-Durr al-Manthur 4: 48, 49, and attributed it to Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh, and I have not found it in any other places than these two.]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This statement which Ibn Zayd made in the interpretation of this verse is a statement far from the interpretation of the verse, along with its contradiction of the views of those whose statements we have mentioned from the people of interpretation (ta'wil).
That is because he made the "hu" (his) in His statement ﴿for him are guardians﴾ refer to the Messenger of God ﷺ, though no mention of him has preceded in the verse before it, nor in the one before that, unless he intended to return it to His statement ﴿You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide, for him are guardians﴾. If that is what he meant, then it is far-fetched, because of the verses between them without any mention of a report about the Messenger of God ﷺ.
And if that is the case, then its reference back to "man," in His statement ﴿and whoever is hidden by night﴾, is closer, because it comes before it and the report follows about it.
Given that, the sense of the speech is: "It is the same among you, O people, whether one conceals speech or speaks it aloud before your Lord, and whether one is hidden by his wickedness and doubt in the darkness of the night, and goes freely, moving about in the light of day, protected by his troops and guards who guard him from the people of obedience to God, from preventing him from what comes of that, and from carrying out the limit of God upon him." And that is His statement ﴿they guard him from the command of God﴾.
* *
As for His statement ﴿Indeed God does not change what is in a people until they change what is in themselves﴾, He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed God does not change what is in a people﴾, of well-being and blessing, so that He removes that from them and destroys them, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾ of that through wronging one another and transgressing against one another, and then His punishment and His change descend upon them.
* *
As for His statement ﴿And when God intends evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾, He says: and when God intends, for these who hide by night and go freely by day, who have troops and protection before them and behind them, guarding them from the command of God, destruction and disgrace in the immediate life of this world, ﴿there is no turning it back﴾: that is, none can avert that from them except God. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿And they have, apart from Him, no governor﴾, that is: and there is not for these people [the "hu" and "mim" in "for them" refer to the people mentioned in His statement ﴿when God intends evil for a people﴾] ﴿apart from Him, any governor﴾, meaning: any governor who has charge of them and has authority over their affairs and their punishment.
* *
Some scholars of the Arabic language used to say: "al-Su'": is ruin. And they used to say: every leprosy, leucoderma, blindness and great affliction is "su'" with the first letter dammed. And when its first letter is fathed, it is a verbal noun from "su'tu." And from it is their saying "a man of evil" (rajul sau'). [This is the text of the words of Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 324.]
The grammarians disputed the meaning of His statement ﴿and whoever is hidden by night and goes freely by day﴾.
Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the meaning of His statement ﴿and whoever is hidden by night﴾ is "and whoever is apparent by night," from their saying "akhfaytu al-shay'" when I made it apparent, as Imru' al-Qays said:
If you conceal the disease, we will not reveal it; and if you stir up war, we will not sit idle. [Diwan: 16, and al-Lisan (kh-f-a), and others, and it will come in the tafsir 16: 114 (Bulaq), with a slight difference in the transmission.]
And he said: and it has been recited, ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Surah Ta-Ha: 15], in the sense of: make it apparent.
And he said, concerning His statement ﴿and goes freely by day﴾, that "al-sarib" is the one who hides himself, as if he directed it to the meaning that he has entered into a "sarab" by day, concealing himself. ["al-Sarab" (with two fathas): a hole beneath the earth.]
* *
Some of the grammarians of Basra and Kufa said: the meaning of that is only: ﴿and whoever is hidden﴾, that is, concealed by night, from the concealment; ﴿and goes freely by day﴾: and goes away by day, from their saying "sarabat al-ibil ila al-ra'y," which is the going of the camels to the pastures and their going out to them.
And it was said: "al-Surub" is in the evening, and "al-Surah" is in the morning.
* *
They also disputed the feminine form of "mu'aqqibat," since it is an attribute of non-females.
Some of the grammarians of Basra said: it was made feminine because of the abundance of that from them, like "nassaba" and "allama," and then it was made masculine because the referent is masculine, so he said "yahfazunahu."
* *
Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: it is only "malaika mu'aqqiba" (a group of angels), and then "mu'aqqibat" was made plural, so it is a plural of a plural; then it was said "yahfazunahu," because it refers to the angels.
* *
Our statement on the meaning of "the one hidden by night and the one going freely by day" has already been given above. [See what passed, pp. 366–368.]
As for what we have mentioned from the grammarians of Basra on this, it is a view which, though it has a basis in the speech of the Arabs, is contrary to the view of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil). And it is sufficient as evidence of its corruption that it departs from the view of all of them. [The context of the speech: "so the statement ... is contrary to the statement of the people of interpretation."]
* *
As for "al-mu'aqqibat," in the speech of the Arabs "al-ta'qib" is return after beginning, and coming back to a thing after turning away from it, from the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Then he turned back, retreating, and did not return [yu'aqqib]﴾, that is: he did not come back. And as Salama ibn Jandal said:
And we turned our horses back upon their traces, returning, with hooves worn from beginning and returning. [Diwan: 8; Sharh al-Mufaddaliyyat: 227, a famous qasida, and its transmission: "And we turned our horses back on their courses, returning," which is the better of the two transmissions, while in the printed edition it was "fi athariha." And his saying "adraajuha" means: from whence they came, they went. "Rujuʿ" is the plural of "rajī'," which is the animal made lean by travel. "Kas al-sanabik" is the plural of "akas," which is the hoof worn down by long travel, that is, its hooves were worn away by the length of the journey. "Al-bad'" is the first raid, and "al-ta'qib" is the return from a raid, or the second raid after the first.]
That is: in a second raid they "returned"; and as Tarafa said:

I have been displeased with you, [[Poetry of the six pre-Islamic poets: 334. "Dhunub" is a large bucket that holds water. He means: "I was angry and displeased with you, yet you returned with the sweet affection without its bitterness, so my heart became pure toward you again."]]
By his words "fa-'aqqabtum," he means: you returned.

The feminine form is used in our view, and it describes the guards who watch over the one who hides by night and the one who goes openly by day, because it was meant as "ḥaras mu'aqqibah" (guards in succession). Then "al-mu'aqqibah" was made plural, so it is said "mu'aqqibāt," and this is the plural of the plural of "al-mu'aqqib," and "al-mu'aqqib" is the singular of "al-mu'aqqibah," as Labid said:

Until he hurried in the morning journey to water, and desire for it stirred him, the pursuit of the one who returns again and again for his right, the wronged one.

[[Diwan, poem no. 16, verse 26; Lisan (ʿaqb). This is from verses describing a wild ass. The explanation of the verse is lengthy, but in summary: the ass "hurried in the morning journey" (tahajjara fi al-rawaḥ), meaning he hastened in the morning to the water; "hajahu" means that love of water moved him, so he hurried to it like one seeking his right who pursues it again and again; this is the "mu'aqqib."
"Al-mazlum" is in the nominative case as an epithet of "al-mu'aqqib" according to meaning, while "al-mu'aqqib" is in the genitive in form; its meaning is that he is the agent of "ṭalab" (pursuit).]]
"Mu'aqqibāt" is its plural. Then he said "yaḥfazūnahu" (they guard him), so the report is returned to the masculine form for the guards and the troops.

* *

As for His words, ﴿They guard him from the command of God﴾, the scholars of Arabic grammar differed about its meaning.

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: its meaning is: for him are successive guards from the command of God who guard him, and they are not from his command. "Yaḥfazūnahu" [they guard him] is a clarification inserted by the context, and it is only an inversion of word order. He said: and "yaḥfazūnahu" means that guarding is from the command of God and by His permission, just as you say to a man, "I answered you from your supplication to me, and by your supplication to me."

* *

And some of the grammarians of Basra said: the meaning of that is: they guard him from the command of God, just as they said, "He fed me from hunger, and against hunger," and "He clothed me from nakedness, and from nakedness."

We have already shown earlier that the most correct interpretation of this is that His words ﴿they guard him from the command of God﴾ describe the guards of the one who hides by night, and they guard him thinking that they repel the command of God from him. So God, may He be exalted, informed that those guards are of no benefit to him at all when His command comes, saying: ﴿And when God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back, and they have no protector besides Him.﴾

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 12–13 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope, and produces the heavy clouds﴾ [12] ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels too, out of awe of Him. And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾ [13].

Abu Ja'far said: His exalted remembrance says: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾, meaning: the Lord is the One who shows His servants the lightning. And His saying ﴿He﴾ is a reference to His name, majestic is His praise.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "lightning" (al-barq) earlier, and we mentioned the difference of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) concerning it, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [See the explanation of "lightning" above, 1: 342–346.]

* *

His saying ﴿as a fear﴾ means: a fear for the traveller from its harm. This is because "lightning" in this place means water, as:

20251 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Salim Abu Jahdam, client of Ibn Abbas, informed us, saying: Ibn Abbas wrote to Abu al-Jald asking him about "lightning", and he said: "Lightning" is water. [The report 20251: Musa ibn Salim, Abu Jahdam, is trustworthy, but his narration from Ibn Abbas is mursal (broken), previously mentioned under no. 434. And Abu al-Jald is Jaylan ibn Farwa al-Asadi, trustworthy, passed under nos. 434, 723, 1913.]

* *

His saying ﴿and as a hope﴾ means: and a hope for the one who stays at home, that it will rain and he will benefit. As:

20252 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope﴾: it means a fear for the traveller on his journeys, fearing its harm and hardship; ﴿and as a hope﴾ for the one who stays at home, hoping for its blessing and benefit, and longing for the provision of God.

20253 – Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿fear and hope﴾: fear for the traveller, and hope for the one who stays at home.

* *

His saying: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾: it stirs up the heavy clouds with rain and originates them.

* *

It is said of this: Allah "anshaa" the cloud when He originates it, and the cloud "nasha'a" when it begins to arise, rising (nash'an).

* *

The word "clouds" (al-sahab) in this place, although it is in singular form, is plural, its singular being "sahaba". That is why He said "the heavy" (al-thiqal), describing it with a plural adjective. If it had come as "al-sahab al-thaqil" it would have been permissible, treating the word "sahab" as singular, as it was said: (Who has made for you from the green tree fire) [Surah Ya-Sin: 80].

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said so:

20254 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Shababa narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾: he said: those that contain water.

20255 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20256 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20257 – ... He said: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20258 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾, he said: those that contain water.

* *

His saying: ﴿and the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the meaning of thunder (al-ra'd) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [See the explanation of "thunder" above, 1: 338–342.]

* *

It has been mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he heard the sound of thunder, would say:

20259 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Kathir ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: Ja'far narrated to us, saying: We have been informed that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he heard the sound of loud thunder, said: "O God, do not kill us with Your wrath, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that." [The report 20259: Ahmad narrated it with this wording in the Musnad, no. 5763, from the hadith of Ibn Umar; al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, no. 721, and my brother, al-Sayyid Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, takhrij'd it in the Musnad.]

20260 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from his father, from a man, from Abu Hurayra, raising the hadith: that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise."

20261 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' al-Bahili narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali (may God be pleased with him), that when he heard the sound of thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify." [The report 20261: Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' ibn Qays al-Yashkuri al-Bahili. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "He is one who has gone from hadith, a rejected transmitter, not to be occupied with; in my view he lies upon Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and God knows best." Ahmad said: "Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' is worth nothing; we tore up his hadith and abandoned his hadith long ago." He is biographed in al-Kabir 4/2/26, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/370, Mizan al-I'tidal 3: 163, and Lisan al-Mizan 6: 23.]

20262 – ... He said: Isma'il ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify." [The report 20262: al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, no. 722, at length. As for "al-Hakam ibn Aban al-Adani", the scholars of hadith have spoken regarding the argument from his good narrations; Ibn Khuzayma so said in his Sahih, and he is trustworthy, God willing. Ibn Hibban said: "He sometimes erred." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/334, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/113.]

20263 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ya'la ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu Sakhra narrate from al-Aswad ibn Yazid, that he would say, when he heard the thunder: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify" — or "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels out of His awe." [The report 20263: Ya'la ibn al-Harith ibn Harb al-Muharibi is trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/418, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/304. Abu Sakhra is Jami' ibn Shaddad al-Muharibi, trustworthy, passed under no. 17982; and my opinion is that he did not hear from al-Aswad ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, but rather heard it from his brother Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, and Abd al-Rahman heard from his brother.]

20264 – ... He said: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father; and Abd al-Karim, from Tawus, that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify."

20265 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Maysara, from al-Awza'i, who said: Ibn Abi Zakariyya used to say: whoever says, when he hears the thunder: "Glory be to God and by His praise," a thunderbolt will not strike him. [The report 20265: "Ibn Abi Zakariyya" is Abd Allah ibn Abi Zakariyya al-Khuza'i al-Shami, Abu Yahya, one of the jurists of the people of Damascus, a contemporary of Makhul, a trustworthy Successor of little narration, a warrior. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/163, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/62.]

* *

The meaning of His saying: ﴿and the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is that the thunder magnifies God and extols Him, so it praises Him with His attributes, and declares Him free of what the people of polytheism ascribe to Him, and of what they describe Him with, such as taking a consort and a son. Exalted is our Lord and sanctified.

* *

His saying: ﴿out of His awe﴾ means: and the angels glorify God out of fear and dread of God. [See the explanation of "khifa" (awe) above, 13: 353 / 15: 389.]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary, with sufficient evidence, and we mentioned the narrations concerning it. [See the explanation of "thunderbolt" above, 2: 82, 83 / 9: 359 / 13: 97.]

* *

The people have differed concerning who this verse was revealed about.

Some of them said: It was revealed about a certain disbeliever who spoke of God, exalted and sanctified be He, in a manner unbefitting to mention Him, so God sent a thunderbolt upon him which destroyed him.

Mention of those who said so:

20266 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Affan narrated to us, saying: Aban ibn Yazid narrated to us, saying: Abu Imran al-Juni narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Suhar al-Abdi, that it reached him that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) sent to a tyrant calling him, and he said: "Tell me about your Lord: is He gold, or silver, or pearl?" He said: While he was disputing with them, God sent a cloud which thundered, and God sent a thunderbolt upon him which took away the top of his skull, and God revealed this verse: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾. [The report 20266: Affan is Affan ibn Muslim al-Saffar, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed many times, the last under no. 20091. Aban ibn Yazid al-Attar is trustworthy, God willing, passed many times. Abu Imran al-Juni is Abd al-Malik ibn Habib al-Azdi, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed under nos. 80, 13042, 17413. Abd al-Rahman ibn Suhar ibn Sakhr al-Abdi had a companionship with his father; he is a trustworthy Successor, narrated from his father, biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/244. This is a mursal report with a sound chain.]

20267 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: A Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Tell me about your Lord: of what is He, of pearl or of ruby? Then a thunderbolt came and seized him, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾.

20268 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20269 – ... He said: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Hashim narrated to us, saying: Sayf narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from Abu Ayyub, from Ali, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, tell me about this One you call to: is He a ruby, or gold, or what is He? He said: So a thunderbolt descended upon the questioner and burned him, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾ to the end of the verse. [The report 20269: "Ishaq" is Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Abdi al-Razi, who settled in al-Rayy, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed many times, the last under no. 16940. As for "Abd Allah ibn Hashim", he was mentioned in a chain like this under nos. 7329, 7938, 12128, and I said at the end of them, "I do not know who he is," but I now lean toward it being Abd Allah ibn Hashim al-Kufi, a resident of al-Rayy, biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/196. As for "Sayf", he is Sayf ibn Umar al-Dabbi, the akhbari, author of the Futuh, and he is weak, of discarded hadith, worth nothing; he has passed many times, the last under no. 12203, and passed in this very same chain under nos. 7329, 7938, 12128. A similar one will come under nos. 20273, 20282, 20286. This is a munkar chain.]

20270 – Muhammad ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Abi Sara al-Shaybani narrated to me, saying: Thabit al-Bunani narrated to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) once sent a man to a man from the pharaohs of the Arabs, saying: "Call him to me." He said: O Messenger of God, he is more insolent than that! He said: "Go to him and call him." He said: So he came to him and said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) calls you!" He said: "Who is the Messenger of God? And what is God? Is He of gold, or of silver, or of copper?" He said: So the man went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "Return to him and call him." He said: So he went to him and repeated to him, and he returned the same answer as the first. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "Return to him and call him!" He said: So he returned to him. While they were exchanging words between them, God sent a cloud right over his head, and it thundered, and a thunderbolt fell from it, which took away the top of his skull, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾. [The report 20270: Muhammad ibn Marzuq is Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Marzuq al-Bahili, the teacher of al-Tabari, trustworthy, passed under nos. 28, 8224, 17249. Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Wahhab al-Hajabi is trustworthy and truthful, passed under no. 7911. Ali ibn Abi Sara al-Shaybani, who is also called Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sara, is a shaykh weak in hadith. Al-Bukhari said: "There is scrutiny concerning his hadith." Abu Dawud said: "People have abandoned his hadith." Ibn Hibban said: "Munkar narrations predominated in his transmission, so he deserves to be abandoned." Al-Uqayli said: "Ali ibn Abi Sara narrated from Thabit al-Bunani, and no one follows him in it; then he narrated for him from Thabit from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾," then he said: "No one follows him in it except one who is like him or close to him." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/189, Mizan al-I'tidal 2: 226, and he mentioned this hadith with this chain and its full wording, counting it among the hadiths that were denounced against him. So this is a very weak chain. Al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7: 42: "Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar narrated it, and the men of al-Bazzar are the men of the Sahih, except Dilam ibn Ghazwan, who is trustworthy."]

* *

Others said: It was revealed about a man among the disbelievers who denied the Qur'an and called the Prophet (ﷺ) a liar.

Mention of those who said so:

20271 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: It has been reported to us that a man denied the Qur'an and called the Prophet (ﷺ) a liar, so God sent a thunderbolt upon him which destroyed him, and God, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning him: ﴿and they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾.

* *

Others said: It was revealed about Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a, who had intended to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he and Amir ibn al-Tufayl.

Mention of those who said so:

20272 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: It was revealed — meaning His saying: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾ — concerning Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a, because Arbad and Amir ibn al-Tufayl ibn Malik ibn Ja'far came before the Prophet (ﷺ), and Amir said: "O Muhammad, shall I embrace Islam and become your successor after you?" He said: "No!" He said: "Then shall I be over the people of the camel-hair tents, and you over the people of the settled towns?" He said: "No!" He said: "Then what is it?" He said: "I will give you the reins of horses to fight upon, for you are a horseman." He said: "Or are not the reins of horses in my hand? By God, I will fill them against you with horsemen and infantry from the Banu Amir!" He said to Arbad: "Either you distract him for me and I strike him with the sword, or I distract him for you and you strike him with the sword." Arbad said: "Distract him for me and I will strike him." [In the manuscript and the printed edition: "akfiyuhu" (I distract him), and the correct reading is what I have established.] Then Ibn al-Tufayl said: "O Muhammad, I have a need of you." He said: "Come near!" He kept drawing near and the Prophet (ﷺ) kept saying: "Come near," until he placed his hands on his knees and leaned over him, and Arbad drew the sword, and drew out a little of it. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw its gleam, he sought refuge with a verse he used to seek refuge with, so Arbad's hand stiffened upon the sword, and God sent upon him a thunderbolt which burned him. That is the saying of his brother:

I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rising of the Simak and the Lion stars...
The lightning and the thunderbolts bereaved me of the horseman on the day of distress, the stout one.

[The poem, its interpretation and its takhrij have passed above, p. 381, note 3.]

* *

I have already mentioned before the report of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, with something similar to this story. [It is the report no. 20250.]

* *

His saying: ﴿and they dispute about God﴾ means: those whom God struck with the thunderbolts struck them while they were in their contention about God, exalted and mighty, against His Messenger (ﷺ). [See the explanation of "al-mujadala" (disputation) above, 15: 402, note 1, and the references there.]

* *

His saying: ﴿and He is mighty in strength﴾: God, exalted is His remembrance, says: God is severe in His contest against those who transgress against Him, act haughtily, and persist in their disbelief in punishment.

* *

"Al-mihal" is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "I contended with so-and-so, and I contend against him in contention and mihal." Its verb form is "mahalat amhalu mahlan", when a man exposes another man to what will destroy him; and from it is his saying: "wa mahilun musaddaq" [and a plaintiff who is believed]. [This is a hadith of Jabir (may God be pleased with him) from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Qur'an is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and a plaintiff whose claim is believed; whoever makes it his forerunner, it leads him to Paradise, and whoever makes it behind his back, it drives him to the Fire." Narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih 1: 287, no. 124, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad took its takhrij there. It is in Majma' al-Zawa'id 1: 17 / 7 / 164, and it is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, but its chain is weakened. See Amali al-Qali 2: 269, with other wording. This report is well known from Ibn Mas'ud, although its sound form is with Jabir.] And from it is the saying of al-A'sha of Banu Tha'laba:

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 13, verses 12–13 (part 2 of 2)**

*Farʿ naba' yahtazzu fī ghuṣni al-majdi… ghazīru al-nadā shadīdu al-miḥāl*
("A branch of a nab' tree quivering on the bough of glory… abundant in generosity, mighty in stratagem.") [Diwanه: 10; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1: 325; Lisan (m-ḥ-l); and others.]

The *nabʿ* is a tree that grows on the summit of a mountain. Its wood is yellow, firm, and heavy in the hand, and when it ages it turns red. Bows (*qisiyy*) are made from it, and it is the best wood for them, since it combines both firmness and flexibility. The *arz* is strength.

This is how Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā recited it, as I was told on the authority of ʿAlī ibn al-Mughīra from him. The later transmitters, however, recite it thus:

*Farʿ farʿin yahtazzu fī ghuṣni al-majdi… kathīru al-nadā ʿaẓīmu al-miḥāl*

[On the phrase *farʿ farʿ*, derived from the saying "he is the *farʿ* of his people," meaning the noble one among them who raises them (*farraʿahum*) in honour, i.e., surpasses them in nobility. The meaning is: he is a lord of lords. This reading is, in my opinion, the best of the transmitted versions of the line.]

Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā interpreted it and claimed that by *miḥāl* is meant punishment, cunning, and chastisement. From the same usage is the words of another poet: [This is Dhū al-Rumma.]

*Wa-labsin bayna aqwāmin fa-kullun*
*aʿadda lahu al-shaghāzibā wa-al-miḥālā*

[Diwan: 445; Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 326; Amali al-Qali 2: 268; Lisan (sh-gh-z-b), (m-ḥ-l); and others. This is from his qasida in praise of Bilal ibn Abi Burda ibn Abi Musa al-Ashʿari, and this verse is the core of his praise. He says after it:

*Wa-kulluhum aladdu akhū kiẓāẓin*
*aʿadda li-kulli ḥāli al-qawmi ḥālā*

*Abarra ʿalā al-khuṣūmi fa-laysa khaṣmun*
*wa-lā khaṣmāni yaghlibuhu jidālā*

*Qaḍayta bi-marratin fa-aṣabta minhu*
*fuṣūṣa al-ḥaqqi fa-nfaṣala infiṣālā*

*Al-labs* is the confusion of a matter, and it is its difficulty. *Al-shaghāzib* is the plural of *shaghzaba*, which means deceit, a ruse, and a stratagem. Its origin is a wrestler seizing another's leg in order to throw him down. *Abarra* means he rose above and overcame. *Qaḍā bi-marratin* means he judged with strength and firmness. *Fuṣūṣ al-ḥaqq* means its core and its knot. This is masterful speech on disputation and judgement.]

\* \*

Those who interpret (*ahl al-taʾwīl*) said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said this:

20273. Al-Muthannā told me: Isḥāq told us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāshim told us: Sayf told us, on the authority of Abū Rawq, on the authority of Abū Ayyūb, on the authority of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in seizing."
[Athar 20273: see the comment on the earlier athar no. 20269.]

20274. Aḥmad ibn Isḥāq told us: Abū Aḥmad told us: Isrāʾīl told us, on the authority of Abū Yaḥyā, on the authority of Mujāhid regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in might."

20275. Bishr told us: Yazīd told us: Saʿīd told us, on the authority of Qatāda regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "That is, power and cunning."

20276. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā told us: Muḥammad ibn Thawr told us, on the authority of Maʿmar, on the authority of al-Ḥasan regarding ﴿mighty in strength﴾: "It means destruction." He said: "When it is destructive (*maḥl*), it is severe." And Qatāda said: "Severe in cunning."

20277. Al-Ḥārith told me: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told us: a man told us, on the authority of ʿIkrima regarding ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah, and He is mighty in strength﴾: "The dispute of Arbad." [In the printed edition: "He said: al-miḥāl is the dispute of Arbad," which is corrupt speech; the manuscript is correct.] ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "What befell Arbad from the thunderbolt."

20278. Al-Qāsim told us: al-Ḥusayn told us: Ḥajjāj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Ibn ʿAbbās said: severe in *ḥawl* (power and strength)."

20279. Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb told us: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in power, and *al-miḥāl* is power."

\* \*

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Ṭabarī) said: The saying we have mentioned from Qatāda concerning the interpretation of *al-miḥāl* is that it means stratagem (*ḥīla*). The saying Ibn Jurayj transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās indicates that both of them read ﴿وَهُوَ شَدِيدُ المَحَالِ﴾ with a fatḥa on the *mīm*, because the verbal noun of *ḥīla* does not come as *miḥāl* with a kasra on the *mīm*. However, it may come in the pattern *mafʿala* from it, becoming *maḥāla*. From this is the saying: "A man is defeated, without a doubt (*lā maḥāla*)." [This is a proverb mentioned by al-Maydani 2: 221, and by Abu Hilal in al-Jamhara: 193, and in Simt al-Ali: 888, and he cited it. Among its poetic instances is the verse of a poet:

*Ḥāwaltu ḥīna ṣaramtanī*
*wa-al-marʾu yaʿjizu lā al-maḥālah*

*Wa-al-dahru yalʿabu bi-al-fatā*
*wa-al-dahru arwagh min thuʿālah*

*Wa-al-marʾu yaksibu māluhu*
*bi-al-shuḥḥi yūrithuhu kalālah*

*Wa-al-ʿabdu yuqraʿu bi-al-ʿaṣā*
*wa-al-ḥurru takfīhi al-maqālah*]

The word *al-maḥāla* in this place is the *mafʿala* form from *ḥīla*. As for the form with a kasra on the *mīm*, it can only be a verbal noun from "*māḥaltu fulānan umāḥiluhu miḥālan*" (I contended with so-and-so in cunning), and *al-mumāḥala* (contention in cunning) is far in meaning from *ḥīla*.

\* \*

Abu Jaʿfar said: I know of no one who read it with a fatḥa on the *mīm*. [In fact al-Aʿraj and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also read it so; see the tafsir of Abu Ḥayyān 5: 376, and Shawadh al-Qiraʾat of Ibn Khālawayh: 66.] Since this is the case, the most correct interpretation is what we have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 12–13 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope, and produces the heavy clouds﴾ [12] ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels too, out of awe of Him. And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾ [13].

Abu Ja'far said: His exalted remembrance says: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾, meaning: the Lord is the One who shows His servants the lightning. And His saying ﴿He﴾ is a reference to His name, majestic is His praise.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "lightning" (al-barq) earlier, and we mentioned the difference of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) concerning it, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [See the explanation of "lightning" above, 1: 342–346.]

* *

His saying ﴿as a fear﴾ means: a fear for the traveller from its harm. This is because "lightning" in this place means water, as:

20251 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Salim Abu Jahdam, client of Ibn Abbas, informed us, saying: Ibn Abbas wrote to Abu al-Jald asking him about "lightning", and he said: "Lightning" is water. [The report 20251: Musa ibn Salim, Abu Jahdam, is trustworthy, but his narration from Ibn Abbas is mursal (broken), previously mentioned under no. 434. And Abu al-Jald is Jaylan ibn Farwa al-Asadi, trustworthy, passed under nos. 434, 723, 1913.]

* *

His saying ﴿and as a hope﴾ means: and a hope for the one who stays at home, that it will rain and he will benefit. As:

20252 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope﴾: it means a fear for the traveller on his journeys, fearing its harm and hardship; ﴿and as a hope﴾ for the one who stays at home, hoping for its blessing and benefit, and longing for the provision of God.

20253 – Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿fear and hope﴾: fear for the traveller, and hope for the one who stays at home.

* *

His saying: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾: it stirs up the heavy clouds with rain and originates them.

* *

It is said of this: Allah "anshaa" the cloud when He originates it, and the cloud "nasha'a" when it begins to arise, rising (nash'an).

* *

The word "clouds" (al-sahab) in this place, although it is in singular form, is plural, its singular being "sahaba". That is why He said "the heavy" (al-thiqal), describing it with a plural adjective. If it had come as "al-sahab al-thaqil" it would have been permissible, treating the word "sahab" as singular, as it was said: (Who has made for you from the green tree fire) [Surah Ya-Sin: 80].

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said so:

20254 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Shababa narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾: he said: those that contain water.

20255 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20256 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20257 – ... He said: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20258 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿and produces the heavy clouds﴾, he said: those that contain water.

* *

His saying: ﴿and the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the meaning of thunder (al-ra'd) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [See the explanation of "thunder" above, 1: 338–342.]

* *

It has been mentioned that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he heard the sound of thunder, would say:

20259 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Kathir ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: Ja'far narrated to us, saying: We have been informed that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he heard the sound of loud thunder, said: "O God, do not kill us with Your wrath, do not destroy us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that." [The report 20259: Ahmad narrated it with this wording in the Musnad, no. 5763, from the hadith of Ibn Umar; al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, no. 721, and my brother, al-Sayyid Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, takhrij'd it in the Musnad.]

20260 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from his father, from a man, from Abu Hurayra, raising the hadith: that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise."

20261 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' al-Bahili narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali (may God be pleased with him), that when he heard the sound of thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify." [The report 20261: Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' ibn Qays al-Yashkuri al-Bahili. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "He is one who has gone from hadith, a rejected transmitter, not to be occupied with; in my view he lies upon Ja'far ibn Muhammad, and God knows best." Ahmad said: "Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa' is worth nothing; we tore up his hadith and abandoned his hadith long ago." He is biographed in al-Kabir 4/2/26, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/370, Mizan al-I'tidal 3: 163, and Lisan al-Mizan 6: 23.]

20262 – ... He said: Isma'il ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify." [The report 20262: al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad, no. 722, at length. As for "al-Hakam ibn Aban al-Adani", the scholars of hadith have spoken regarding the argument from his good narrations; Ibn Khuzayma so said in his Sahih, and he is trustworthy, God willing. Ibn Hibban said: "He sometimes erred." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/334, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/113.]

20263 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ya'la ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu Sakhra narrate from al-Aswad ibn Yazid, that he would say, when he heard the thunder: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify" — or "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels out of His awe." [The report 20263: Ya'la ibn al-Harith ibn Harb al-Muharibi is trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/418, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/304. Abu Sakhra is Jami' ibn Shaddad al-Muharibi, trustworthy, passed under no. 17982; and my opinion is that he did not hear from al-Aswad ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, but rather heard it from his brother Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, and Abd al-Rahman heard from his brother.]

20264 – ... He said: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father; and Abd al-Karim, from Tawus, that when he heard the thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him to whom You glorify."

20265 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Maysara, from al-Awza'i, who said: Ibn Abi Zakariyya used to say: whoever says, when he hears the thunder: "Glory be to God and by His praise," a thunderbolt will not strike him. [The report 20265: "Ibn Abi Zakariyya" is Abd Allah ibn Abi Zakariyya al-Khuza'i al-Shami, Abu Yahya, one of the jurists of the people of Damascus, a contemporary of Makhul, a trustworthy Successor of little narration, a warrior. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/163, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/62.]

* *

The meaning of His saying: ﴿and the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾ is that the thunder magnifies God and extols Him, so it praises Him with His attributes, and declares Him free of what the people of polytheism ascribe to Him, and of what they describe Him with, such as taking a consort and a son. Exalted is our Lord and sanctified.

* *

His saying: ﴿out of His awe﴾ means: and the angels glorify God out of fear and dread of God. [See the explanation of "khifa" (awe) above, 13: 353 / 15: 389.]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary, with sufficient evidence, and we mentioned the narrations concerning it. [See the explanation of "thunderbolt" above, 2: 82, 83 / 9: 359 / 13: 97.]

* *

The people have differed concerning who this verse was revealed about.

Some of them said: It was revealed about a certain disbeliever who spoke of God, exalted and sanctified be He, in a manner unbefitting to mention Him, so God sent a thunderbolt upon him which destroyed him.

Mention of those who said so:

20266 – Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Affan narrated to us, saying: Aban ibn Yazid narrated to us, saying: Abu Imran al-Juni narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Suhar al-Abdi, that it reached him that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) sent to a tyrant calling him, and he said: "Tell me about your Lord: is He gold, or silver, or pearl?" He said: While he was disputing with them, God sent a cloud which thundered, and God sent a thunderbolt upon him which took away the top of his skull, and God revealed this verse: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾. [The report 20266: Affan is Affan ibn Muslim al-Saffar, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed many times, the last under no. 20091. Aban ibn Yazid al-Attar is trustworthy, God willing, passed many times. Abu Imran al-Juni is Abd al-Malik ibn Habib al-Azdi, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed under nos. 80, 13042, 17413. Abd al-Rahman ibn Suhar ibn Sakhr al-Abdi had a companionship with his father; he is a trustworthy Successor, narrated from his father, biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/244. This is a mursal report with a sound chain.]

20267 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: A Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Tell me about your Lord: of what is He, of pearl or of ruby? Then a thunderbolt came and seized him, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾.

20268 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, the like of it.

20269 – ... He said: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Hashim narrated to us, saying: Sayf narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from Abu Ayyub, from Ali, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, tell me about this One you call to: is He a ruby, or gold, or what is He? He said: So a thunderbolt descended upon the questioner and burned him, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾ to the end of the verse. [The report 20269: "Ishaq" is Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Abdi al-Razi, who settled in al-Rayy, trustworthy, narrated by the group, passed many times, the last under no. 16940. As for "Abd Allah ibn Hashim", he was mentioned in a chain like this under nos. 7329, 7938, 12128, and I said at the end of them, "I do not know who he is," but I now lean toward it being Abd Allah ibn Hashim al-Kufi, a resident of al-Rayy, biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/196. As for "Sayf", he is Sayf ibn Umar al-Dabbi, the akhbari, author of the Futuh, and he is weak, of discarded hadith, worth nothing; he has passed many times, the last under no. 12203, and passed in this very same chain under nos. 7329, 7938, 12128. A similar one will come under nos. 20273, 20282, 20286. This is a munkar chain.]

20270 – Muhammad ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Abi Sara al-Shaybani narrated to me, saying: Thabit al-Bunani narrated to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) once sent a man to a man from the pharaohs of the Arabs, saying: "Call him to me." He said: O Messenger of God, he is more insolent than that! He said: "Go to him and call him." He said: So he came to him and said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) calls you!" He said: "Who is the Messenger of God? And what is God? Is He of gold, or of silver, or of copper?" He said: So the man went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "Return to him and call him." He said: So he went to him and repeated to him, and he returned the same answer as the first. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "Return to him and call him!" He said: So he returned to him. While they were exchanging words between them, God sent a cloud right over his head, and it thundered, and a thunderbolt fell from it, which took away the top of his skull, and God revealed: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾. [The report 20270: Muhammad ibn Marzuq is Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Marzuq al-Bahili, the teacher of al-Tabari, trustworthy, passed under nos. 28, 8224, 17249. Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Wahhab al-Hajabi is trustworthy and truthful, passed under no. 7911. Ali ibn Abi Sara al-Shaybani, who is also called Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sara, is a shaykh weak in hadith. Al-Bukhari said: "There is scrutiny concerning his hadith." Abu Dawud said: "People have abandoned his hadith." Ibn Hibban said: "Munkar narrations predominated in his transmission, so he deserves to be abandoned." Al-Uqayli said: "Ali ibn Abi Sara narrated from Thabit al-Bunani, and no one follows him in it; then he narrated for him from Thabit from Anas concerning His saying: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾," then he said: "No one follows him in it except one who is like him or close to him." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/189, Mizan al-I'tidal 2: 226, and he mentioned this hadith with this chain and its full wording, counting it among the hadiths that were denounced against him. So this is a very weak chain. Al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7: 42: "Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar narrated it, and the men of al-Bazzar are the men of the Sahih, except Dilam ibn Ghazwan, who is trustworthy."]

* *

Others said: It was revealed about a man among the disbelievers who denied the Qur'an and called the Prophet (ﷺ) a liar.

Mention of those who said so:

20271 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: It has been reported to us that a man denied the Qur'an and called the Prophet (ﷺ) a liar, so God sent a thunderbolt upon him which destroyed him, and God, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning him: ﴿and they dispute about God, and He is mighty in strength﴾.

* *

Others said: It was revealed about Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a, who had intended to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he and Amir ibn al-Tufayl.

Mention of those who said so:

20272 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: It was revealed — meaning His saying: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾ — concerning Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a, because Arbad and Amir ibn al-Tufayl ibn Malik ibn Ja'far came before the Prophet (ﷺ), and Amir said: "O Muhammad, shall I embrace Islam and become your successor after you?" He said: "No!" He said: "Then shall I be over the people of the camel-hair tents, and you over the people of the settled towns?" He said: "No!" He said: "Then what is it?" He said: "I will give you the reins of horses to fight upon, for you are a horseman." He said: "Or are not the reins of horses in my hand? By God, I will fill them against you with horsemen and infantry from the Banu Amir!" He said to Arbad: "Either you distract him for me and I strike him with the sword, or I distract him for you and you strike him with the sword." Arbad said: "Distract him for me and I will strike him." [In the manuscript and the printed edition: "akfiyuhu" (I distract him), and the correct reading is what I have established.] Then Ibn al-Tufayl said: "O Muhammad, I have a need of you." He said: "Come near!" He kept drawing near and the Prophet (ﷺ) kept saying: "Come near," until he placed his hands on his knees and leaned over him, and Arbad drew the sword, and drew out a little of it. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw its gleam, he sought refuge with a verse he used to seek refuge with, so Arbad's hand stiffened upon the sword, and God sent upon him a thunderbolt which burned him. That is the saying of his brother:

I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rising of the Simak and the Lion stars...
The lightning and the thunderbolts bereaved me of the horseman on the day of distress, the stout one.

[The poem, its interpretation and its takhrij have passed above, p. 381, note 3.]

* *

I have already mentioned before the report of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, with something similar to this story. [It is the report no. 20250.]

* *

His saying: ﴿and they dispute about God﴾ means: those whom God struck with the thunderbolts struck them while they were in their contention about God, exalted and mighty, against His Messenger (ﷺ). [See the explanation of "al-mujadala" (disputation) above, 15: 402, note 1, and the references there.]

* *

His saying: ﴿and He is mighty in strength﴾: God, exalted is His remembrance, says: God is severe in His contest against those who transgress against Him, act haughtily, and persist in their disbelief in punishment.

* *

"Al-mihal" is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "I contended with so-and-so, and I contend against him in contention and mihal." Its verb form is "mahalat amhalu mahlan", when a man exposes another man to what will destroy him; and from it is his saying: "wa mahilun musaddaq" [and a plaintiff who is believed]. [This is a hadith of Jabir (may God be pleased with him) from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Qur'an is an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, and a plaintiff whose claim is believed; whoever makes it his forerunner, it leads him to Paradise, and whoever makes it behind his back, it drives him to the Fire." Narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih 1: 287, no. 124, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad took its takhrij there. It is in Majma' al-Zawa'id 1: 17 / 7 / 164, and it is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, but its chain is weakened. See Amali al-Qali 2: 269, with other wording. This report is well known from Ibn Mas'ud, although its sound form is with Jabir.] And from it is the saying of al-A'sha of Banu Tha'laba:

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 13, verses 12–13 (part 2 of 2)**

*Farʿ naba' yahtazzu fī ghuṣni al-majdi… ghazīru al-nadā shadīdu al-miḥāl*
("A branch of a nab' tree quivering on the bough of glory… abundant in generosity, mighty in stratagem.") [Diwanه: 10; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1: 325; Lisan (m-ḥ-l); and others.]

The *nabʿ* is a tree that grows on the summit of a mountain. Its wood is yellow, firm, and heavy in the hand, and when it ages it turns red. Bows (*qisiyy*) are made from it, and it is the best wood for them, since it combines both firmness and flexibility. The *arz* is strength.

This is how Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā recited it, as I was told on the authority of ʿAlī ibn al-Mughīra from him. The later transmitters, however, recite it thus:

*Farʿ farʿin yahtazzu fī ghuṣni al-majdi… kathīru al-nadā ʿaẓīmu al-miḥāl*

[On the phrase *farʿ farʿ*, derived from the saying "he is the *farʿ* of his people," meaning the noble one among them who raises them (*farraʿahum*) in honour, i.e., surpasses them in nobility. The meaning is: he is a lord of lords. This reading is, in my opinion, the best of the transmitted versions of the line.]

Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā interpreted it and claimed that by *miḥāl* is meant punishment, cunning, and chastisement. From the same usage is the words of another poet: [This is Dhū al-Rumma.]

*Wa-labsin bayna aqwāmin fa-kullun*
*aʿadda lahu al-shaghāzibā wa-al-miḥālā*

[Diwan: 445; Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 326; Amali al-Qali 2: 268; Lisan (sh-gh-z-b), (m-ḥ-l); and others. This is from his qasida in praise of Bilal ibn Abi Burda ibn Abi Musa al-Ashʿari, and this verse is the core of his praise. He says after it:

*Wa-kulluhum aladdu akhū kiẓāẓin*
*aʿadda li-kulli ḥāli al-qawmi ḥālā*

*Abarra ʿalā al-khuṣūmi fa-laysa khaṣmun*
*wa-lā khaṣmāni yaghlibuhu jidālā*

*Qaḍayta bi-marratin fa-aṣabta minhu*
*fuṣūṣa al-ḥaqqi fa-nfaṣala infiṣālā*

*Al-labs* is the confusion of a matter, and it is its difficulty. *Al-shaghāzib* is the plural of *shaghzaba*, which means deceit, a ruse, and a stratagem. Its origin is a wrestler seizing another's leg in order to throw him down. *Abarra* means he rose above and overcame. *Qaḍā bi-marratin* means he judged with strength and firmness. *Fuṣūṣ al-ḥaqq* means its core and its knot. This is masterful speech on disputation and judgement.]

\* \*

Those who interpret (*ahl al-taʾwīl*) said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said this:

20273. Al-Muthannā told me: Isḥāq told us: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāshim told us: Sayf told us, on the authority of Abū Rawq, on the authority of Abū Ayyūb, on the authority of ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in seizing."
[Athar 20273: see the comment on the earlier athar no. 20269.]

20274. Aḥmad ibn Isḥāq told us: Abū Aḥmad told us: Isrāʾīl told us, on the authority of Abū Yaḥyā, on the authority of Mujāhid regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in might."

20275. Bishr told us: Yazīd told us: Saʿīd told us, on the authority of Qatāda regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "That is, power and cunning."

20276. Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā told us: Muḥammad ibn Thawr told us, on the authority of Maʿmar, on the authority of al-Ḥasan regarding ﴿mighty in strength﴾: "It means destruction." He said: "When it is destructive (*maḥl*), it is severe." And Qatāda said: "Severe in cunning."

20277. Al-Ḥārith told me: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told us: a man told us, on the authority of ʿIkrima regarding ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah, and He is mighty in strength﴾: "The dispute of Arbad." [In the printed edition: "He said: al-miḥāl is the dispute of Arbad," which is corrupt speech; the manuscript is correct.] ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "What befell Arbad from the thunderbolt."

20278. Al-Qāsim told us: al-Ḥusayn told us: Ḥajjāj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj regarding ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Ibn ʿAbbās said: severe in *ḥawl* (power and strength)."

20279. Yūnus told me: Ibn Wahb told us: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾: "Severe in power, and *al-miḥāl* is power."

\* \*

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Ṭabarī) said: The saying we have mentioned from Qatāda concerning the interpretation of *al-miḥāl* is that it means stratagem (*ḥīla*). The saying Ibn Jurayj transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās indicates that both of them read ﴿وَهُوَ شَدِيدُ المَحَالِ﴾ with a fatḥa on the *mīm*, because the verbal noun of *ḥīla* does not come as *miḥāl* with a kasra on the *mīm*. However, it may come in the pattern *mafʿala* from it, becoming *maḥāla*. From this is the saying: "A man is defeated, without a doubt (*lā maḥāla*)." [This is a proverb mentioned by al-Maydani 2: 221, and by Abu Hilal in al-Jamhara: 193, and in Simt al-Ali: 888, and he cited it. Among its poetic instances is the verse of a poet:

*Ḥāwaltu ḥīna ṣaramtanī*
*wa-al-marʾu yaʿjizu lā al-maḥālah*

*Wa-al-dahru yalʿabu bi-al-fatā*
*wa-al-dahru arwagh min thuʿālah*

*Wa-al-marʾu yaksibu māluhu*
*bi-al-shuḥḥi yūrithuhu kalālah*

*Wa-al-ʿabdu yuqraʿu bi-al-ʿaṣā*
*wa-al-ḥurru takfīhi al-maqālah*]

The word *al-maḥāla* in this place is the *mafʿala* form from *ḥīla*. As for the form with a kasra on the *mīm*, it can only be a verbal noun from "*māḥaltu fulānan umāḥiluhu miḥālan*" (I contended with so-and-so in cunning), and *al-mumāḥala* (contention in cunning) is far in meaning from *ḥīla*.

\* \*

Abu Jaʿfar said: I know of no one who read it with a fatḥa on the *mīm*. [In fact al-Aʿraj and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also read it so; see the tafsir of Abu Ḥayyān 5: 376, and Shawadh al-Qiraʾat of Ibn Khālawayh: 66.] Since this is the case, the most correct interpretation is what we have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 13, verse 14:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿To Him is the true call. And those they call upon besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who extends his hands toward water so that it reaches his mouth, but it does not reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is not but in error.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: To Him, from among His creation, belongs the true call (al-da'wa al-haqq), and "the call" is "the truth," just as the abode is attributed to the Hereafter in His words: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 109], and we have explained that previously. [See what has passed, pp. 294, 295.]

What is meant by "the true call" is the affirmation of God's oneness and the testimony that there is no god but God.

* *

And the interpreters have explained it in a manner close to what we have said.

Those who said that:

20280- Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Israil narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿the call of truth﴾, he said: "There is no god but God."

20281- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, he said: "The testimony that there is no god but God."

20282- ... He said: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Hashim narrated to us, saying: Sayf narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from Abu Ayyub, from Ali, may God be pleased with him: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, he said: "The affirmation of God's oneness (al-tawhid)." [The report 20282: this chain of narration, which is destroyed (al-halik), has passed several times, the last being no. 20273.]

20283- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, he said: "There is no god but God."

20284- Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said, regarding His words: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, he said: "There is no god but God."

20285- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿To Him is the true call﴾: "There is no god but God; it is not fitting for anyone other than Him. It is not proper to say: 'So-and-so is the god of the Banu so-and-so.'"

* *

As for His words: ﴿And those they call upon besides Him﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: the deities that the polytheists call upon as lords and gods.

* *

As for His words ﴿besides Him﴾, it means: besides God.

* *

What is meant by His words ﴿besides Him﴾ is that the deities fall short of Him, and that they are not gods, and it is not permissible for anyone to be a god except God, the One, the Subduer (al-Qahhar). [See the explanation of "dun" (besides) in the indexes of language, under (dun).] From this is the saying of the poet: [He is Jarir.]

"Do you threaten me from behind the Banu Riyah? ... You lie! Your hands will fall short of me (lataqsurann yadaka duni)."

[Diwan, p. 577; al-Naqa'id, p. 31; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubayda 1:326; al-Adwad of Ibn al-Anbari, p. 58; it will come shortly in the commentary, 13:130 (Bulaq), and it is found in many other places. He satirizes Fudala of the Banu Urayn.]

That is: "Your hands will fall short of me."

* *

As for His words: ﴿They do not respond to them with anything﴾, it means: these deities which these polytheists call upon as gods do not answer them with anything they desire of benefit or repelling of harm. ﴿Except like one who extends his hands toward water﴾, it means: the supplication of one who calls upon the deities does not benefit him, except as the benefit to one who extends his hands toward water by stretching them out to it, without its rising to him in a vessel; rather, it rises to him by his calling to it, his gesturing toward it, and his grasping at it.

* *

The Arabs strike, as a proverb for one who strives for what he cannot attain, the image of one who grasps water. [They said in the proverb: "like one who grasps water"; see Amthal al-Maydani 2:80, and Jamharat al-Amthal, p. 164.] One of them said: [He is Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi.]

"Indeed, I and you, and longing for you, are like one who grasps water whose fingers have not carried it (lam tasqihi anamiluh)."

[From his poem which he composed in prison, when he had prepared an iron blade with which he wanted to assassinate Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him. His poetry is in Khizanat al-Adab 4:80; in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara', p. 145; Tarikh al-Tabari 5:137 / 7:213; the verse is in al-Khizana and in al-Lisan (w-s-q); Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubayda 1:327; Gharib al-Qur'an of Ibn Qutayba, p. 226. His words "lam tasqihi" derive from "wasaqtu al-shay' asquhu wasqan," meaning I carried it.]

By this he means: he has nothing of that in his hand except what is in the hand of one who grasps water, because one who grasps water has nothing in his hand. Another said: [He is al-Ahwas ibn Muhammad al-Ansari.]

"So I have become, of what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand."

[Al-Zahra, p. 183; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubayda 1:327. Before it: "Woe to my regret when I did not return, when she said to me: 'Go forward, and bid us farewell until the forenoon of tomorrow.'" The version in al-Zahra: "other than its remembrance, like one grasping water in the hand." It is a very good version, better than what Abu Ubayda and al-Tabari transmitted.]
